120453.long_answer: The most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which blocks the synthesis of glucocorticoids. The key hormone that becomes deficient is cortisol. Because the body cannot produce adequate cortisol, ACTH levels rise, leading to adrenal hyperplasia and excess androgen production. Clinically, this deficiency is treated with replacement glucocorticoids. Synthetic analogs of cortisol—such as hydrocortisone, prednisone, and prednisolone—are among the most frequently prescribed drugs worldwide due to their broad use in endocrine replacement, inflammation control, and immunosuppression. Thus, the hormone primarily lacking in the common CAH variant and for which a widely used synthetic analog exists is cortisol.

125994.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the CRADD gene (also known as RAIDD) have been shown to cause frontal-dominant polymicrogyria in affected individuals. Biochemically, CRADD is an adaptor protein that interacts with RIPK1 and CASP2 and is required for tumor-necrosis-factor-α (TNFα)-induced activation of the JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase) signaling cascade. Thus, CRADD links the cortical malformation polymicrogyria with JNK pathway activation in response to TNFα.

131415.long_answer: Petrolatum (petroleum jelly) is widely used as an over-the-counter topical emollient to treat xeroderma (dry skin) because it forms an occlusive barrier that reduces transepidermal water loss. The same substance—listed as white petrolatum or petroleum jelly—is the principal lubricating ingredient in many commercial hairball remedies for domestic cats, where it helps the ingested hair pass through the gastrointestinal tract.

139280.long_answer: Ackerman syndrome has occasionally been reported in association with juvenile open-angle glaucoma. This form of glaucoma is rare, arises between childhood and early adulthood, and is classically inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern, matching the description in the question.

147361.long_answer: Lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 gene. The definitive way to establish whether an individual carries one of these variants is to sequence the coding region of FOXC2. The sequencing method first described in 1977 by Frederick Sanger and colleagues—the dideoxy chain-termination or Sanger sequencing test—directly reads the nucleotide sequence of DNA and therefore can reveal the presence or absence of FOXC2 mutations, confirming or excluding the diagnosis of lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome.

149454.long_answer: SIX3 (Sine oculis‐related homeobox 3) is widely described as the “master control” or “master regulator” gene for vertebrate eye development because its activity initiates and coordinates formation of the eye field.  Loss-of-function or other misexpression of SIX3 in humans disrupts early forebrain and midline patterning; such disturbances are a well-established cause of holoprosencephaly (HPE), with clinical presentations that range from very mild to very severe.  Pathogenic SIX3 variants account for a significant proportion of familial and sporadic HPE cases (historically classified as HPE2), demonstrating that improper regulation of this eye-field master gene can lead to the spectrum of holoprosencephaly phenotypes.

153240.long_answer: In the 2016 study that examined the prenatal‐ultrasound characteristics of Limb Body Wall Complex, the investigators documented that the malformation could already be recognised during the first-trimester scan; the earliest case in their series was identified at 11 weeks of gestation. Thus, the study concluded that Limb Body Wall Complex can first be detected at 11 weeks.

154301.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive congenital disorder distinguished by craniofacial malformations (including craniosynostosis), childhood-onset obesity, pre- and post-axial polydactyly, and soft-tissue or osseous syndactyly. Because it shares the triad of polysyndactyly and craniofacial abnormalities with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome, Carpenter syndrome is listed among the principal disorders that clinically overlap with GCPS in differential-diagnosis guides.

167837.long_answer: Jacobsen syndrome—also called 11q terminal deletion disorder—is a rare congenital condition produced by deletions on the long (q) arm of chromosome 11. Affected individuals typically display characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism (e.g., broad nasal bridge, down-slanting palpebral fissures), growth and psychomotor delay, congenital heart defects, hematologic abnormalities such as Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, and multiple other physical and developmental problems.

170431.long_answer: In the WHO clinical staging system for HIV/AIDS, Kaposi sarcoma is listed as a Stage IV condition. The cutaneous or visceral tumors produced by Kaposi sarcoma must be distinguished from several other entities—common differentials cited in clinical manuals include dermatofibrous histiocytoma, pneumocystis-related pulmonary or cutaneous lesions, vascular tumors such as angiomas, and pigmented malignancies like melanoma. Because this differential diagnosis specifically matches the options given, Kaposi sarcoma is the severe symptom referred to in the question.

218487.long_answer: The potassium-sparing diuretic amiloride is routinely used in clinical practice to manage hypertension and is also the primary (first-line) pharmacologic treatment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, particularly when the condition is induced by lithium therapy. Amiloride acts on the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, reducing sodium reabsorption and thereby decreasing the polyuria characteristic of nephrogenic DI while sparing potassium.

229400.long_answer: Hypergammaglobulinemic purpura (also called Waldenström’s purpura) is an uncommon form of recurrent purpura characterized by elevated serum immunoglobulins. Epidemiologic studies show a marked female predominance—about 85 % of reported cases occur in women—making it both rare and distinctly more frequent in the female population.

259072.long_answer: Peyronie’s disease is characterized by the development of fibrous plaques within the tunica albuginea of the penis. These plaques can cause abnormal penile curvature, pain, and interfere with normal blood flow and tissue elasticity, often resulting in erectile dysfunction—defined as the inability to achieve or maintain an erection with sufficient rigidity for satisfactory sexual activity.

280426.long_answer: HLA-B27 is a human leukocyte antigen (MHC class I) allele encoded within the major histocompatibility complex on chromosome 6p21.3. Its presence is routinely tested as an immune marker because it is strongly associated with, and therefore aids in the diagnosis of, juvenile idiopathic arthritis—particularly the enthesitis-related and axial subtypes.

314843.long_answer: In hereditary spastic paraplegia, an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern means the disease-causing gene is located on the X chromosome and is recessive. Because males have only one X chromosome, a single mutated copy causes the disorder, so they are affected. Females have two X chromosomes; when only one carries the mutation, the normal copy on the other X usually prevents disease expression, making them asymptomatic carriers who can pass the mutation to their sons.

324488.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene (BCL-6 corepressor) on Xp11.4. The same BCOR gene is also responsible for Lenz microphthalmia syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by microphthalmia/anophthalmia, skeletal anomalies, and developmental delay. Thus, the recessively inherited disease caused by the same gene as OFCD syndrome is Lenz microphthalmia syndrome.

331013.long_answer: The SERPINA1 gene, situated on chromosome 14q32, encodes the serine-protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT). AAT’s main physiological role is to neutralize neutrophil elastase and related proteases. When AAT is deficient, elastase activity in connective-tissue–rich organs, including the aortic wall, is left unchecked, leading to excessive degradation of elastin fibers. This accelerated elastin breakdown weakens the aortic media and has been associated with a higher incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysm formation. Thus, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can promote pathological elastin loss in the aorta and elevate AAA risk.

356129.long_answer: The folate-antagonist antimetabolite methotrexate, first synthesized in 1947 by Subbarao and colleagues, is widely accepted as the first-line agent for primary intraocular (vitreoretinal) lymphoma. High-dose systemic methotrexate or intravitreal methotrexate injections achieve cytotoxic folate depletion in malignant lymphocytes and have become the standard initial therapy recommended in oncology and ophthalmology guidelines for this disease.

362433.long_answer: Mowat–Wilson syndrome is a congenital disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ZEB2 gene. Along with distinctive facial features, Hirschsprung disease, intellectual disability, and agenesis of the corpus callosum, a high proportion of affected individuals develop recurrent, unprovoked seizures. The neurological disorder defined by such recurrent seizures is epilepsy, making epilepsy a common comorbidity in people with Mowat–Wilson syndrome.

366445.long_answer:
Hydroquinone is a depigmenting (whitening) agent that inhibits the enzyme tyrosinase, thereby reducing melanin synthesis. Dermatologists commonly prescribe 2–4 % hydroquinone creams to fade post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, including the brown macules that follow phytophotodermatitis.

Because prolonged or inappropriate use can cause adverse effects such as irritant dermatitis, exogenous ochronosis and potential carcinogenicity, the European Union has banned hydroquinone from over-the-counter cosmetic products (Directive 76/768/EEC and subsequent amendments). Medical-prescription preparations are still allowed, but it can no longer be included in ordinary cosmetic skin-lightening products sold in Europe. Thus, hydroquinone is the whitening agent referred to in the question.

438711.long_answer: The World Health Organization and UNICEF recommend zinc supplementation (10–20 mg daily for 10-14 days) for children suffering from acute gastroenteritis because it shortens the duration and severity of diarrhoeal episodes and reduces subsequent morbidity. Zinc is an essential trace element required for over 300 enzymatic reactions, DNA and protein synthesis, and immune function. Adequate zinc status is critical during both prenatal development (organogenesis, neural and immune system formation) and postnatal growth (linear growth, cognitive development, immune competence). Thus, zinc fulfills both criteria mentioned: it is routinely given as a supplement in paediatric gastroenteritis and is indispensable for normal prenatal and postnatal development.

472843.long_answer: The principal red blood cell receptor recognized by Plasmodium falciparum PfEMP1 during rosetting is complement receptor 1 (CR1/CD35). The CR1 gene is located in the long arm of human chromosome 1 (1q32). Therefore, the red-blood-cell receptor to which PfEMP1 binds is encoded on chromosome 1.

483894.long_answer: Type XVII collagen, also known as BP180 or BPAG2, is an integral hemidesmosomal transmembrane protein that is the principal autoantigen in bullous pemphigoid. The gene that encodes type XVII collagen is COL17A1, located on chromosome 10q24. This gene’s product forms the 180-kDa component of hemidesmosomes, and autoantibodies directed against it lead to the subepidermal blistering characteristic of the disease.

486804.long_answer: Brachydactyly type A1 (BDA1) is caused by pathogenic variants in the Indian hedgehog gene (IHH). IHH encodes one of the three mammalian Hedgehog ligands and functions at the center of the Hedgehog signaling pathway that regulates chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation during endochondral ossification. Disruption of this pathway through IHH mutations specifically produces the characteristic shortening of the middle phalanges seen in BDA1, making this form of brachydactyly directly linked to Hedgehog signaling.

494387.long_answer: Methotrexate is a folic-acid antagonist (antifolate) that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. It is widely used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug in chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) when first-line treatments fail, and it is also a standard systemic therapy for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Its dual efficacy in these inflammatory conditions makes methotrexate the antifolate medication employed for both CRMO and psoriasis.

496183.long_answer: The cells first identified in the bursa of Fabricius (an avian organ absent in mammals) are B lymphocytes.  In X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia), mutations in the gene encoding Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) lead to markedly reduced or absent BTK protein levels in B-cell precursors.  The deficiency of this specific tyrosine kinase blocks B-cell maturation, causing the characteristic disorder.

504058.long_answer: The protein is GAIP-interacting protein, C-terminus 1 (GIPC1, also called synectin). Human GIPC1 is composed of 333 amino acids, has an apparent molecular mass of ~36 kDa, and contains a single centrally positioned PDZ domain (residues ≈101-185). Biochemical studies demonstrated that GIPC1 binds to the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif of the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR), making it the scaffold protein that satisfies all features described in the question.

514385.long_answer: L-glyceric acidemia (also called L-glyceric aciduria or primary hyperoxaluria type II) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GRHPR gene, which encodes glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase. Defective GRHPR impairs the conversion of hydroxypyruvate to D-glycerate and glyoxylate to glycolate, leading to accumulation and systemic elevation of L-glycerate. This condition is distinct from D-glyceric acidemia, which involves a different enzymatic defect (glycerate kinase/GLYCTK).

522257.long_answer: Hajdu–Cheney syndrome is characterized by multiple skeletal abnormalities, one of which is the presence of supernumerary, small bone islands that form within the cranial sutures. These accessory ossicles are classically called Wormian bones—also referred to as sutural or intrasutural bones—because they occur between the normal skull bones along the suture lines. Their occurrence in excess is a well-documented radiographic feature of the disorder.

539437.long_answer: The WFS1 (wolframin) gene is best known for causing Wolfram syndrome, but more than thirty different WFS1 mutations have also been documented in individuals who have isolated (nonsyndromic) sensorineural hearing loss. Nonsyndromic forms account for roughly three-quarters (≈75 %) of all hereditary hearing-loss cases, distinguishing them from the remaining syndromic causes. Thus, the condition linked both to about 75 % of hearing-loss cases and to the >30 hearing-loss-specific WFS1 mutations is nonsyndromic hearing loss.

546137.long_answer: Hydrochlorothiazide is a classic thiazide diuretic that paradoxically reduces polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by inducing mild extracellular-fluid volume contraction, which enhances proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water. Clinical guidelines and pharmacology texts cite it as the first-line pharmacologic therapy for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In addition, hydrochlorothiazide is listed under the ‘Diuretics’ section of the World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines, confirming its global importance and accessibility.

568641.long_answer: Absent tibia-polydactyly-arachnoid cyst syndrome presents with limb malformations similar to those seen in disorders caused by mutations in the HOXD gene cluster on chromosome 2q31. Because of this phenotypic overlap, researchers analysed the coding sequence of the chromosome-2 homeobox gene HOXD13 in affected patients. Sequencing revealed no pathogenic variants, demonstrating that HOXD13 is not abnormal in individuals with this syndrome.

571688.long_answer: The stethoscope is the acoustic medical device physicians place on the chest or other body surfaces to perform auscultation—listening to internal sounds from the heart, lungs, intestines, and blood flowing through arteries and veins. In 1887, French physicians M. Cuffer and M. Barbillon used a stethoscope during auscultation to describe the characteristic mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that occurs in patients with mitral valve prolapse. This landmark observation established the stethoscope as an essential tool for diagnosing valvular heart disorders as well as a broad range of cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal conditions.

581924.long_answer: Probst bundles are longitudinal fiber tracts that form when the commissural fibers of the corpus callosum fail to cross the midline. Their presence is a classic neuroradiologic sign of agenesis of the corpus callosum (complete or partial absence of this structure). In Infantile Spasms–Broad Thumbs Syndrome (also called Say-Field syndrome), this rare birth defect—corpus callosum agenesis—has been repeatedly documented, explaining the characteristic Probst bundles seen in affected individuals.

593091.long_answer: Among the heterogeneous features of osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis are congenital cardiac anomalies – for example atrial or ventricular septal defects and pulmonary valve stenosis. Congenital heart disease is likewise a classic finding in Holt–Oram syndrome, Noonan syndrome and Alagille syndrome. Therefore, the symptom common to osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis and all three of these other syndromes is the presence of a congenital heart defect.

602194.long_answer: Ionizing radiation is defined by its ability to carry enough energy to remove (ionize) electrons from atoms and molecules. Sources such as therapeutic X-rays, γ-rays, and radiation from atomic bomb explosions deliver this high-energy radiation. Large epidemiologic studies of survivors of atomic bombings, patients who received cranial radiotherapy, and workers exposed occupationally have consistently shown increased incidences of gliomas, meningiomas, and other central nervous system tumors. Because of this clear dose-related association, ionizing radiation is recognized by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and other health authorities as a proven environmental risk factor for brain cancers.

622659.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant and mood-stabilising drug first synthesized in 1953 by the Swiss chemist Walter Schindler at J.R. Geigy AG in Basel. Prolonged therapy with carbamazepine has been shown to lower serum biotin levels and reduce biotinidase activity, leading to clinically significant biotin deficiency in some long-term users. This association is well documented in nutritional and pharmacological studies, establishing carbamazepine as a medication that can precipitate biotin deficiency with extended use.

716881.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (also known as acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by craniosynostosis, polysyndactyly, brachydactyly, soft-tissue syndactyly, obesity, and other malformations. Pathogenic biallelic mutations in the small GTP-binding protein gene RAB23 (located on chromosome 6p12) have been identified as a major molecular cause of this syndrome. Thus, Carpenter syndrome is the RAB23-related condition classically associated with brachydactyly.

722142.long_answer: Genomic studies of sporadic meningiomas have shown that somatic mutations in the gene encoding TNF receptor-associated factor 7 (TRAF7) occur in roughly 20–25 % of tumors. These TRAF7 mutations commonly co-occur with mutations in KLF4 (in secretory meningiomas) or are found alone in other non-NF2 meningioma subtypes, making TRAF7 one of the most frequently altered genes in this disease.

728614.long_answer: Bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II (BMPR2) is the principal gene in which pathogenic variants cause heritable/primary pulmonary (arterial) hypertension.  Separate families carrying heterozygous BMPR2 mutations have also been reported with the skeletal malformation brachydactyly type A2, characterised by shortening of the middle phalanges of the index (and often little) fingers.  Thus, BMPR2 is the gene that is etiologically linked to both primary pulmonary hypertension and type A2 brachydactyly.

744208.long_answer: Ovarian cancer frequently presents with vague gastrointestinal and pelvic symptoms—persistent abdominal bloating or distension, altered bowel habits (constipation, diarrhoea), pelvic or abdominal pain, early satiety, and sometimes abnormal or post-menopausal vaginal bleeding. Because these manifestations closely mimic those of irritable bowel syndrome, many women are initially misdiagnosed with IBS, leading to delayed recognition of ovarian malignancy. Consequently, ovarian cancer is the malignancy most commonly confused with IBS when patients report bloating, bowel-habit changes, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.

771231.long_answer: Ischiopatellar dysplasia (also called small-patella syndrome) is an autosomal-dominant skeletal malformation characterized by hypoplastic or absent patellae, pelvic and foot anomalies. Genetic studies have shown that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the TBX4 gene are responsible for this disorder. TBX4 encodes a T-box transcription factor that is critically required for embryonic hindlimb development; it is expressed in the developing hindlimb bud and in the allantois, the embryonic structure that gives rise to the umbilical cord and umbilicus. Disruption of TBX4 therefore affects both hindlimb morphogenesis and umbilical formation, explaining the clinical features of ischiopatellar dysplasia when the gene is mutated.

814670.long_answer: Quinine and related cinchona alkaloids are drugs employed in the treatment of both malaria and, in combination regimens, babesiosis. Excessive dosing or chronic high-level exposure to these medications leads to the well-defined toxicity syndrome called cinchonism (or quinism). Cinchonism is characterized by symptoms such as tinnitus, hearing and visual disturbances, headache, nausea, and CNS effects, and it represents the classic condition resulting from quinine overdose.

822308.long_answer: Thin basement membrane disease and IgA nephropathy (also called Berger disease) are the two disorders most often responsible for persistent hematuria in otherwise asymptomatic patients. While thin basement membrane disease is due to collagen IV abnormalities that make the glomerular basement membrane abnormally thin, IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial deposition of immunoglobulin A. Both conditions commonly present with microscopic (and occasionally macroscopic) hematuria without edema, hypertension, or impaired renal function at initial presentation, making them the leading causes of isolated hematuria.

859993.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an iminostilbene anticonvulsant that acts primarily by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. It was first synthesized and characterized in Basel, Switzerland, by the company J. R. Geigy in the 1950s, and has since become a widely used medication for epilepsy, trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder. Among its rare but serious adverse effects is the development of severe cutaneous reactions, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell’s syndrome). Because of this well-documented association, carbamazepine is the anticonvulsant most commonly linked to Lyell’s syndrome in clinical reports and pharmacovigilance data.

879885.long_answer: Equinophobia is classified as a specific phobia.  The first-line, evidence-based ‘talk therapy’ for specific phobias is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).  In CBT, a therapist helps the person identify and challenge distorted thoughts about horses and gradually confront the feared stimulus through controlled exposure, relaxation training and cognitive restructuring.  Numerous clinical guidelines (e.g., American Psychiatric Association, NICE) recommend CBT as the most effective psychotherapy for treating specific phobias such as equinophobia.

908283.long_answer: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease (pseudogout) can be managed with colchicine. Colchicine is a recognized substrate for both the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter and the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme. Drugs that inhibit either P-gp or CYP3A4 (e.g., clarithromycin, ketoconazole, verapamil) can markedly raise systemic colchicine concentrations, leading to serious toxicity. Because of these well-established interactions, dosing adjustments or alternative therapies are required when colchicine is combined with strong P-gp or CYP3A4 inhibitors.

963020.long_answer: Yellow fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic fever for which the World Health Organization recommends a single-dose live-attenuated 17D vaccine. WHO policy states that all individuals aged nine months and older living in, or traveling to, areas where yellow fever is endemic should receive this vaccine, as it confers long-lasting immunity and is critical for outbreak prevention.

986088.long_answer: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the DMD gene located at Xp21 on the X chromosome. Several X-linked forms of hereditary spastic paraplegia (e.g., SPG1 / L1CAM at Xq28 and SPG2 / PLP1 at Xq22) also map to genes on the X chromosome. Therefore, both conditions involve mutations in genes situated on the X chromosome.

150243.long_answer: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (also called marfanoid craniosynostosis syndrome) is a rare congenital multiple-anomaly disorder produced by heterozygous mutations in the SKI gene on chromosome 1p36. Affected individuals show craniosynostosis, marfanoid habitus, arachnodactyly—extremely long, slender “spider fingers”—and other connective-tissue and skeletal abnormalities. The association of SKI gene mutations with this characteristic phenotype is well established in the medical genetics literature, making Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome the correct answer.

176281.long_answer: The scientist who first carried out chorionic villus sampling is the Italian biologist-geneticist Giuseppe Simoni. His official curriculum states that he earned his Laurea in Biological Sciences (the Italian equivalent of a biology degree) at the Università degli Studi di Milano—known in English as the University of Milan—before leading the team that introduced CVS in 1983. Therefore, the university at which he obtained his biology degree was the University of Milan.

285796.long_answer: Pelvic lipomatosis is a rare disorder marked by benign, disproportionate overgrowth of mature adipose tissue within the pelvis. It occurs predominantly in middle-aged to older Black men who are obese (body-mass index ≥30 kg/m²). The massive perivesical fat narrows the pelvis and indents the urinary bladder, producing the classic “pear-shaped” or “teardrop” bladder appearance on CT or IVU imaging. These characteristic epidemiologic features and imaging findings make pelvic lipomatosis the recognized answer.

506722.long_answer: A median sternotomy is the standard surgical approach in cardiac and many thoracic operations. The surgeon makes a single vertical midline incision through the skin and divides the sternum longitudinally to spread the chest, giving direct access to the heart, great vessels, and anterior lungs. Because the skin and subcutaneous tissues over the sternum are incised and subjected to tension during healing, patients are at risk of developing hypertrophic or keloid scars along the mid-chest incision line.

654558.long_answer: Lenz–Majewski syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PTDSS1 gene, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1 (PSS1). PSS1 catalyzes the base-exchange reaction that converts phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylserine. The constitutively active mutant enzyme drives excessive synthesis of its product, leading to cellular accumulation of the phospholipid phosphatidylserine.

666700.long_answer: Vitamin E comprises several tocopherols and tocotrienols, but the form with the highest biological activity in humans is α-tocopherol (especially the RRR-α-tocopherol stereoisomer). In the European Union food-additive system, α-tocopherol is assigned the code E307, while mixed tocopherol extracts are E306 and other tocopherol isomers have different numbers. Therefore, the E number corresponding to the most bioactive form of vitamin E is E307.

970294.long_answer: The parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by kissing bugs, causes Chagas disease. In chronically infected individuals who later become immunosuppressed by HIV, reactivation of T. cruzi most commonly produces a severe meningoencephalitis. This is marked by intense inflammation and the formation of necrotizing, pus-filled abscesses within the brain parenchyma, visible on imaging and confirmed histologically. Hence, the organ affected is the brain.

139521.long_answer: Amiodarone, a class III anti-arrhythmic agent, is well documented to deposit iodinated phospholipids in pulmonary tissue. These deposits lead to the characteristic picture of lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages and parenchymal inflammation, a pattern described pathologically and radiologically as exogenous lipid (lipoid) pneumonia. Hence, amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic medication classically associated with exogenous lipid pneumonia.

284028.long_answer: Fair-haired children may present with loose anagen hair syndrome, a disorder in which the anagen (growing) hairs are poorly anchored and shed easily. One therapeutic approach is to improve follicular nutrition by increasing scalp blood flow. Minoxidil, originally an antihypertensive arterial vasodilator, is applied topically for this purpose. By dilating dermal blood vessels, minoxidil raises local blood supply, delivering more oxygen and nutrients to the hair matrix cells, thereby stimulating thicker, stronger anagen hairs. Clinical reports document successful use of 2–5 % topical minoxidil in fair-haired children with this condition, making minoxidil the drug of choice to enrich hair cells through enhanced vascular perfusion.

295910.long_answer: The adrenal cortex gives rise to adrenocortical adenomas, which are the most frequent benign tumors found in the adrenal glands. A large proportion of these tumors, especially cortisol-producing adenomas, harbor activating mutations in genes that regulate the cyclic AMP (cAMP)–dependent protein kinase A (PKA) pathway—for example, somatic mutations in PRKACA or inactivating mutations in GNAS or PRKAR1A. These molecular alterations lead to constitutive PKA signaling, driving cell proliferation and hormone excess. Because of both their prevalence and their well-established link to dysregulated cAMP-PKA activity, adrenocortical adenomas represent the prototypic benign adrenal tumor associated with cAMP-dependent protein kinase A signaling.

298228.long_answer: The VPS33B gene (Vacuolar Protein Sorting-Associated Protein 33B), whose biallelic pathogenic variants cause arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome, is mapped to cytogenetic band 15q26 on human chromosome 15. This chromosomal assignment has been confirmed by linkage analysis, fluorescence in-situ hybridization, and genome assemblies (e.g., GRCh38: chr15: 100,064,801-100,095,373). Hence, VPS33B resides on chromosome 15.

308498.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome results from defects in proteins required for ribosomal RNA synthesis. The small subunit common to RNA polymerases I and III—POLR1C (DNA-directed RNA polymerase I and III subunit C)—physically associates with other Pol I components, including CD3EAP (also called ASE-1), POLR1E and POLR1D, to form the functional transcription complex. Pathogenic loss-of-function mutations in the POLR1C gene disrupt this interaction network, impair rRNA transcription, and are a well-established cause of Treacher Collins syndrome (designated TCS type 3). Hence, the protein that interacts with CD3EAP, POLR1E and POLR1D and whose mutation produces Treacher Collins syndrome is POLR1C.

419700.long_answer: Baruch Samuel Blumberg shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the Hepatitis B virus. Hepatitis B virus is the prototype species of the family Hepadnaviridae, a group of small, enveloped DNA viruses that infect the liver of humans and other animals. Consequently, the virus family that includes Blumberg’s infectious agent is Hepadnaviridae.

459609.long_answer: The larynx is the organ that contains the vocal cords. When laryngeal carcinoma spreads hematogenously, the lungs are by far the most frequent site of distant metastases, reflecting both vascular drainage patterns and the high susceptibility of pulmonary tissue to lodging of circulating tumor cells. Clinical series consistently report the lung as the initial and predominant organ involved in distant spread from laryngeal cancer.

480829.long_answer: In babesiosis, the intra-erythrocytic protozoan Babesia spp. may divide into four merozoites arranged at right angles to one another, producing a tetrad that resembles a Maltese cross. On a peripheral blood smear this appears as four “V”-shaped inclusions converging centrally within a red blood cell—a distinctive diagnostic feature of babesiosis.

527168.long_answer: Ellis–Van Creveld syndrome (EVC), also called chondroectodermal dysplasia, is a rare autosomal-recessive skeletal and ectodermal disorder produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the EVC gene (or its paralog EVC2). The EVC proteins localize to the base of primary cilia and participate in Hedgehog signalling; their dysfunction disrupts ciliary structure and signaling pathways, so the condition is classified within the growing group of primary cilia–related disorders known as ciliopathies.

583819.long_answer: The human EDARADD (EDAR-associated death domain) gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 1, specifically at cytogenetic band 1q42–q43. This chromosomal localization has been established through linkage analysis and refined by genomic sequencing projects such as the Human Genome Project and Ensembl/NCBI annotations.

623637.long_answer: The specific type of pneumoconiosis responsible for about 3,600 deaths worldwide in 2015 was asbestosis. Asbestosis is a chronic fibrotic lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibers, leading to progressive pulmonary scarring and respiratory failure. Global Burden of Disease 2015 estimates attribute roughly 3,600 deaths to this condition, distinguishing it from other pneumoconioses such as silicosis or coal workers’ pneumoconiosis.

659460.long_answer: Myhre syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SMAD4 gene. The canonical human SMAD4 protein that this gene encodes is composed of 552 amino acids, as documented in reference protein databases (e.g., UniProt entry Q13485). Therefore, the gene product contains 552 amino acids.

660741.long_answer: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a mitochondrial co-factor sold as a dietary supplement rather than an FDA-approved drug. Small clinical studies in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and other forms of congestive heart failure have shown that supplemental CoQ10 can improve myocardial energy production, ejection fraction, and functional status. Because of these observed benefits, clinicians sometimes recommend CoQ10 to individuals with dilated cardiomyopathy who are experiencing heart failure, even though the supplement has not yet received FDA approval for this indication.

686876.long_answer: A 2016 global nutrition review by UNICEF, WHO and the World Bank estimated that about 52.9 million children under five years of age were affected by wasting—acute malnutrition manifested by low weight-for-height and loss of muscle and fat tissue.  Wasting is recognised as being associated with a variety of disorders that impair energy storage or utilisation, including glycogen-storage disease type VI (Hers’ disease), in which impaired hepatic glycogen breakdown can lead to poor growth and loss of body mass.  Thus, the condition linked to Hers’ disease and reported to affect roughly 52.9 million young children worldwide in 2016 is wasting (acute malnutrition).

722978.long_answer: Cuffer and Barbillon identified the mid-systolic click simply by auscultation with a stethoscope.  The stethoscope was invented by the French physician René-Théophile-Hyacinthe Laennec in 1816; hence the device they used in their 1887 observations had been in existence since 1816.

837230.long_answer: The TK2 gene (thymidine kinase 2, mitochondrial) lies on chromosome 16q22.1. Mutations in TK2 produce the myopathic form of mitochondrial DNA-depletion syndrome type 2. Infants carrying pathogenic TK2 variants appear normal during infancy and early childhood, but around two years of age they begin to show generalized, progressive muscle weakness that steadily worsens. The disorder currently has no curative or disease-modifying treatment, only supportive care, matching the scenario described.

847295.long_answer: In the European Union and many other jurisdictions, a disorder is considered rare when it affects fewer than 1 person in every 2,000. Conditions such as the microcornea-glaucoma-absent-frontal-sinus syndrome fall under this definition, meaning no more than about 1 individual per 2,000 people would typically be affected.

865090.long_answer: Human cytomegalovirus (CMV), a betaherpesvirus that possesses an icosahedral capsid with T=16 symmetry, is the foremost non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural deafness and consequent balance/ambulatory difficulties acquired via vertical (in utero) transmission.

879116.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome (KFDCA) is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive disorder; to date only six patients, all originating from Mexico, have been reported in the medical literature. Mexico won its War of Independence against the Spanish Empire with the signing of the Treaty of Córdoba and the declaration of the Acta de Independencia on 28 September 1821. Therefore, the year in which the country achieved independence from Spain is 1821.

888878.long_answer: Magnetic-resonance imaging studies of patients with X-linked Say–Meyer syndrome consistently describe an abnormally thin corpus callosum—the largest white-matter commissural tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres. This hypoplasia of the corpus callosum is a characteristic neuroanatomical finding associated with the syndrome’s developmental delay and other clinical features.

920528.long_answer: Van den Ende–Gupta syndrome (VDEGS) is an autosomal-recessive malformation syndrome that was first described in 1992 in two siblings born to consanguineous Arab parents—the only cases known at that time, making it an exceptionally rare genetic disorder.  Core manifestations include characteristic facial features (blepharophimosis, narrow beaked nose, everted lower lip) and multiple skeletal anomalies such as radial-head dislocation, camptodactyly, slender ribs, hypoplastic scapulae and, very commonly, congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).  Subsequent reports have confirmed the strong association of VDEGS with clubfoot, and mutations in the SCARF2 gene have been identified as its molecular cause.

974208.long_answer: Hodgkin lymphoma makes up roughly 10 % of all lymphoma cases. About 40–50 % of Hodgkin lymphoma tumors contain Epstein-Barr virus genomes, indicating a frequent association with EBV infection.

979905.long_answer: Lymph nodes are small, bean- or kidney-shaped organs of the lymphatic system. In pancreatic cancer, the TNM staging system assigns great importance to whether regional lymph nodes (peripancreatic, celiac, hepatoduodenal, superior mesenteric, etc.) contain metastatic deposits. Cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic ultrasound, and surgical sampling therefore focus closely on these kidney-shaped structures to determine nodal involvement and overall stage.

995113.long_answer: Gómez–López-Hernández (cerebellotrigeminal-dermal) syndrome has been linked to pathogenic variants in the EXT2 gene.  EXT2 is situated on chromosome 11p11-p12 and codes for exostosin-2, which pairs with exostosin-1 to form the two-subunit heparan-sulfate polymerase enzyme.  Mutations disrupting EXT2 therefore implicate this gene in the pathogenesis of Gómez–López-Hernández syndrome.

106578.long_answer: Fanconi anemia–associated bone-marrow failure can be managed temporarily with pharmacologic agents. Androgens (e.g., oxymetholone) are often combined with hematopoietic growth factors that are naturally occurring glycoproteins capable of stimulating the proliferation, differentiation, and maturation of blood-cell precursors. This class of glycoproteins is collectively termed colony-stimulating factors (CSFs), which include agents such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Administering CSFs alongside androgens can transiently improve cytopenias until definitive therapy (e.g., hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation) is undertaken.

117785.long_answer: Basilar invagination refers to the upward displacement of the odontoid process into the foramen magnum at the cranio-vertebral junction. The odontoid process is part of the second cervical vertebra, the axis (C2). Thus, the bone specifically involved in basilar invagination is the axis (C2 vertebra).

134630.long_answer: The yellow pigment that produces the characteristic discoloration seen in jaundice is bilirubin, a tetrapyrrole breakdown product of heme. Until recently it was thought to occur only in animals, but chemical analysis showed that the white bird-of-paradise plant, Strelitzia nicolai, accumulates the same molecule in its orange aril tissues. This makes Strelitzia nicolai the first plant species confirmed to contain bilirubin, the very pigment responsible for jaundice’s yellow hue.

157149.long_answer: Cystic hygromas (lymphangiomas) in the neck most often arise in the posterior triangle, deep to or surrounding the sternocleidomastoid. Dissection in this area places the spinal accessory nerve—cranial nerve XI, which courses superficially across the posterior triangle to innervate the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius—at particular risk of traction or transection injury during removal of the mass.

224427.long_answer: Pasireotide (marketed in the United States as Signifor and Signifor LAR) is the only medication that has received specific U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the treatment of pituitary-dependent Cushing’s disease in adults who are either not candidates for curative pituitary surgery or who have persistent or recurrent disease after pituitary surgery. The somatostatin analogue binds with high affinity to somatostatin receptor subtype 5 on corticotroph adenomas, suppressing excessive ACTH secretion and thereby lowering cortisol levels, and its labeling explicitly limits the indication to this patient population.

230703.long_answer: The fragile site located at Xq27.2 is classified as an aphidicolin-inducible common fragile site. Exposure of human cells to the fungal antibiotic aphidicolin, an inhibitor of DNA polymerase α/δ, produces replication stress and consistently triggers chromosomal breaks or gaps at this locus. Cytogenetic studies that map fragile site expression have therefore long used aphidicolin to reveal the Xq27.2 breaks, establishing it as the specific antibiotic inducer for this region.

237915.long_answer: Cysteine, the amino acid whose sulfhydryl groups form the disulfide bonds that stabilize many protein structures, is produced in humans by trans-sulfuration of methionine through the enzymes cystathionine β-synthase and cystathionine γ-lyase. Both enzymes require pyridoxal-5′-phosphate, the active co-enzyme form of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). When the diet is deficient in vitamin B6, pyridoxal-5′-phosphate levels fall, these B6-dependent reactions slow, and endogenous synthesis of cysteine is markedly reduced. Thus a deficiency of the essential nutrient vitamin B6 specifically impairs the body’s ability to make the disulfide-bond-forming amino acid cysteine.

252895.long_answer: In Anton syndrome, patients are cortically blind yet insist they can see. This unawareness of, or failure to acknowledge, their deficit is a specific example of anosognosia—a condition first detailed by the French neurologist Joseph Babinski in 1914 to describe patients who deny or are unaware of their neurological impairments.

260402.long_answer: The single most frequent large-scale mitochondrial DNA rearrangement in both chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) and Kearns–Sayre syndrome is the 4,977-base-pair (≈4.9-kb) deletion that spans nucleotide positions ~8,470–13,447 of the mitochondrial genome. This “common deletion” is detected in roughly one-third of CPEO cases and is the predominant deletion reported in Kearns–Sayre syndrome, making it the hallmark molecular lesion of these disorders.

290551.long_answer: Individuals with xeroderma pigmentosum avoid sunlight to limit UV-induced DNA damage, which markedly reduces cutaneous synthesis of vitamin D. Consequently they often take vitamin D supplements. The metabolically active (hormonally active) form of vitamin D in the body is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol—also known as calcitriol—which exerts the biological effects of the vitamin on calcium and phosphate homeostasis.

408853.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type X is caused by a deficiency of the cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase (protein kinase A). This enzyme normally phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn activates glycogen phosphorylase to promote glycogen breakdown. When PKA is deficient, this signaling cascade is blunted, leading to impaired glycogenolysis, hepatic glycogen accumulation, and the clinical picture of GSD X.

515320.long_answer: Barakat syndrome, also called HDR (Hypoparathyroidism-Deafness-Renal dysplasia) syndrome, is characterized by defects in the kidneys, which are the body’s principal blood-filtering organs. Patients typically exhibit renal dysplasia, hypoplasia, or other structural and functional kidney abnormalities, making the kidneys the organ most commonly affected in this condition.

545881.long_answer: An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses the normal high-resistance arteriolar bed. Because blood flows directly from the high-pressure arterial system into the low-pressure venous system, total peripheral resistance falls sharply. The reduced afterload, together with the marked rise in venous return, forces the heart to pump a much larger volume of blood, so cardiac output rises substantially—especially if the fistula involves a large artery.

559411.long_answer: The condition is Early Myoclonic Encephalopathy (EME), an epileptic encephalopathy that begins in the neonatal period or within the first three months of life. It is distinguished by fragmentary, erratic myoclonic jerks and violent myoclonic spasms, leading to frequent, drug-resistant seizures and severe developmental impairment.

632188.long_answer: The described presentation—primary amenorrhea in a phenotypic female who has normal breast development and pubic hair because her ovaries function normally, but who lacks a uterus and upper vagina—is classic for Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. MRKH is a congenital Müllerian agenesis/duplication defect in which the Müllerian ducts fail to develop, resulting in absence or rudimentary formation of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina. Because the ovaries originate from a different embryologic source (the genital ridge), they develop and function normally, producing estrogen that drives secondary sexual characteristics. Hence, affected individuals are 46,XX with fully developed secondary sex traits yet experience primary amenorrhea due to the absent uterine outflow tract.

656117.long_answer: Immune (erythroblastosis) hydrops fetalis is most commonly triggered by Rh-D incompatibility in which an Rh-negative mother forms antibodies against fetal Rh-positive red cells. Administering Anti-D immunoglobulin (Rho(D) immune globulin) to every Rh-negative woman after any potential fetomaternal hemorrhage—routinely at 28–30 weeks’ gestation and within 72 hours postpartum—destroys fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes in the maternal circulation before the mother can mount an immune response. This preventive injection blocks maternal allo-immunisation and thereby prevents the immune-mediated hemolytic disease that can progress to hydrops fetalis in subsequent pregnancies.

689063.long_answer: Cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) is clustered on human chromosome 15q24, belongs to the xenobiotic-metabolising CYP1 family, and catalyses several oxidative reactions including ring-hydroxylation of toluene; hence it is a key enzyme in toluene and broader xenobiotic metabolism.

695539.long_answer: Oxymetholone is an anabolic androgenic steroid that stimulates proliferation and differentiation of hematopoietic progenitor cells, thereby enhancing the growth and maturation of red cells, neutrophils and platelets. Because these effects can partially counter the pancytopenia characteristic of Fanconi anemia, oxymetholone is routinely employed as a supportive (non-curative) pharmacologic therapy for patients with this disorder.

709773.long_answer: The epidemic disease that first appeared in November 2002 was Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). The initial cluster was reported in Guangdong Province, China, and the illness rapidly spread internationally during 2002-2003. Clinically, SARS is caused by the SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and is marked by high fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and laboratory findings that commonly include leukopenia with pronounced lymphocytopenia. These hematologic abnormalities, together with its sudden emergence and global transmission, define the SARS epidemic that began in November 2002.

714294.long_answer: Moyamoya disease 2 (MYMY2) was first linked to a missense change in the RNF213 gene: a G→A transition at nucleotide 14576 that replaces arginine with lysine at position 4810 of the protein (commonly written p.R4810K, also described as p.R4859K in a longer isoform). This founding East-Asian mutation was the initial genetic alteration proven to cause autosomal-dominant Moyamoya disease 2.

725163.long_answer: The described condition is adermatoglyphia, sometimes nick-named the “immigration delay disease.” It is an extremely rare autosomal-dominant disorder reported in only about ten families worldwide. Affected individuals are born without epidermal ridges (fingerprints) and often develop transient neonatal blisters and facial milia. Genetic studies have shown that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations affecting an alternative, skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene on chromosome 4 are responsible for the phenotype.

771022.long_answer: Vibrio vulnificus is a halophilic, Gram-negative rod that naturally inhabits warm marine and brackish waters found in estuaries, coastal areas, and salt- or brackish ponds. When introduced through breaks in the skin or mucosa, it can produce a fulminant soft-tissue infection with necrotizing fasciitis. Numerous case reports and reviews document V. vulnificus as an established, though uncommon, etiologic agent of Fournier gangrene, the necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genital region. Its association with seawater exposure and the rapid, life-threatening progression of the infection make V. vulnificus the prototypical marine bacterium implicated in Fournier gangrene.

782966.long_answer: The definitive, disease-modifying therapy frequently employed for life-threatening bone-marrow disorders such as acute leukemia, lymphoma, myelodysplastic syndromes, and certain solid-tumor malignancies is hematopoietic stem-cell (bone marrow) transplantation. In this procedure a patient’s diseased or dysfunctional marrow is ablated with high-dose chemotherapy and/or total-body irradiation, then replaced by infusion of healthy hematopoietic stem cells obtained from a compatible donor (allogeneic) or from the patient previously collected (autologous). The new stem cells migrate to the marrow cavities and re-establish normal blood-cell production. Although usually reserved for malignant or otherwise fatal marrow failure states, the same transplant technique is also considered for selected patients with severe, transfusion-dependent sideroblastic anemia when conventional medical therapy is ineffective or complications such as iron overload threaten survival, because successful engraftment can permanently correct the underlying erythroid defect.

793771.long_answer: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of the Hepatitis B virus was awarded to Dr. Baruch S. Blumberg in 1976. Blumberg completed his medical training at Columbia University’s College of Physicians and Surgeons, receiving his M.D. in 1951. Thus, the university where he earned his medical degree is Columbia University.

910648.long_answer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles that house hydrolytic enzymes responsible for degrading glycosaminoglycans, sphingolipids, and other macromolecules. Beyond their classic catabolic role, lysosomes participate in regulated secretion, plasma-membrane repair, apoptosis, nutrient and energy sensing, and multiple cell-signaling pathways. When specific lysosomal enzymes that break down glycosaminoglycans are genetically deficient, undegraded ‘mucopolysaccharides’ accumulate inside lysosomes, producing the group of lysosomal storage disorders collectively known as the mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler, Hunter, Sanfilippo syndromes). Thus, malfunction of lysosomes underlies the pathogenesis of mucopolysaccharidoses.

933016.long_answer: Tonsillectomy—the surgical excision of the palatine tonsils—is routinely performed to manage recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and is also part of first-line surgical therapy for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea. Because the glossopharyngeal nerve and its lingual branches that carry taste fibers to the posterior third of the tongue run close to the tonsillar bed, they can be stretched, bruised, or partially severed during dissection. This neural injury may lead to postoperative taste disturbances, including dysgeusia (distortion or alteration of taste). Although usually transient, dysgeusia is a well-recognized potential complication specifically associated with tonsillectomy.

954297.long_answer: Varicella-zoster virus can infect and inflame cerebral arteries (VZV vasculopathy), precipitating an ischemic stroke. This complication typically presents with focal neurologic deficits such as dizziness and dysarthria (brainstem–cerebellar involvement) together with hemiparesis and paresthesia (unilateral motor and sensory impairment), making stroke the hallmark severe complication described.

970726.long_answer: One of the five additional features frequently reported alongside MASA syndrome is hydrocephalus—a condition in which cerebrospinal fluid accumulates within the brain’s ventricles, leading to their enlargement and raised intracranial pressure.

166341.long_answer: The first recognized clinical case of uniparental disomy (reported by Spence et al., 1988) involved maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 in a patient with cystic fibrosis. Human chromosome 7 contains about 159 million base pairs; as detailed in genome reference data (e.g., NCBI, Genetics Home Reference), this amount corresponds to roughly 5 percent of the total DNA present in human cells. Therefore, the duplicated chromosome in that landmark UPD case represents about 5 % of the cellular DNA.

182169.long_answer: Recurrent respiratory (laryngeal) papillomatosis produces multiple squamous papillomas that arise most frequently on the true vocal cords—the stratified-squamous-covered glottic mucosa, especially around the anterior commissure. Although lesions can spread to other supraglottic or subglottic sites, the true vocal folds are by far the commonest location for the benign tumors.

218896.long_answer: The lesion most frequently encountered near the mental foramen following surgical injury to a peripheral nerve is the traumatic (also called amputation) neuroma. It is a reactive proliferation of nerve fibers and supporting tissue that develops when a severed or damaged nerve attempts to regenerate, producing a benign nodular mass in the area of the prior trauma.

287123.long_answer: The neurons that are progressively lost in cerebellar degeneration are Purkinje cells. These large cerebellar neurons were first described by the Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkinje in 1837. Subsequent neuropathological studies linked their degeneration to many cerebellar ataxias, but the initial discovery of the cell type itself dates to 1837.

355170.long_answer: Achard–Thiers syndrome combines diabetes mellitus with excessive androgen production, leading to masculinizing manifestations such as hirsutism, acne, and virilization in affected women. The standard pharmacologic strategy for reducing these androgen-related symptoms is to give drugs that antagonize androgen action. Anti-androgen agents—e.g., spironolactone, cyproterone acetate, flutamide, or other androgen-receptor blockers—diminish peripheral androgen effects and thereby alleviate hirsutism and other virilizing signs. Consequently, anti-androgens are the class of drugs most commonly prescribed for symptomatic control in women with Achard–Thiers syndrome.

408733.long_answer: In the evaluation of loin pain hematuria syndrome, one of the conditions that must be excluded is lupus nephritis secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  The classical complement component-1q (C1q) genes—C1QA, C1QB and C1QC—are clustered on chromosome 1 at cytoband 1p36.12.  Deficiency or polymorphic variation in these genes is a well-established genetic association with the development of SLE.  Thus, systemic lupus erythematosus is both part of the differential diagnosis for loin pain hematuria syndrome and is genetically linked to the cytoband 1p36.12.

442535.long_answer: Carotenoid pigments (the carotenes and xanthophylls) are embedded in and around the protein cores of photosystem I and photosystem II. Besides enlarging the light-harvesting range, they protect chlorophyll from photo-oxidative damage. When a plant cannot synthesize carotenoids—because of genetic mutations or inhibitors—chlorophyll is rapidly destroyed by light, and the tissues become white or �albino.� Hence, deficiency of carotenoids is the molecular cause of albinism in such plants.

619326.long_answer: In the single infant described with Cortés-Lacassie syndrome, progressive renal failure developed secondary to the metabolic defect. The authors of the case report noted that early liver transplantation (to correct the underlying enzymatic defect) or, alternatively, dialysis to remove the accumulating metabolites could potentially have halted or delayed the advance of this renal failure.

627918.long_answer: Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome (opercular syndrome) can occasionally be produced not by permanent structural lesions but by bilateral propagation of epileptic discharges that transiently inactivate the frontal opercular cortices.  When the epilepsy is medically intractable, disconnective surgery that prevents the rapid spread of ictal activity from one hemisphere to the other can abolish the opercular seizures and the associated negative motor phenomena.  Corpus callosotomy – sectioning the corpus callosum either partially (usually the anterior two-thirds) or completely – is a well-established neurosurgical treatment for refractory epilepsy.  By interrupting interhemispheric spread, a callosotomy can eliminate the bilateral opercular involvement, leading to complete resolution of the Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome that was being produced by those epileptic discharges.  Case reports document full recovery of voluntary facial, lingual, pharyngeal and masticatory movements after corpus callosotomy in such patients, confirming the effectiveness of this procedure in reversing FCMS when it is seizure-induced.

770213.long_answer: Potocki–Lupski syndrome is a rare microduplication of chromosome 17p11.2. One of its namesakes is Dr. James R. Lupski, a professor of molecular and human genetics at Baylor College of Medicine. Dr. Lupski is internationally recognized for his research on the hereditary neuropathy Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, and the syndrome bears his name along with that of Dr. Lorraine Potocki because of their joint description of the disorder.

820147.long_answer: The French dermatologist Robert Degos (1904–1987) first recognized malignant atrophic papulosis, now called Degos disease, as a distinct clinical entity in 1941. A decade later he consolidated his clinical experience and observations in a comprehensive textbook. Published in 1953, this work was titled “Dermatologie,” and it is in this book that Degos again described and discussed the disease that now bears his name.

828118.long_answer: In dermatological terminology a solid, palpable lesion that is larger than 1 cm in diameter is called a nodule. During the early stage of Eumycetoma, patients develop small, firm subcutaneous swellings that usually exceed 1 cm; these lesions are therefore termed nodules.

132019.long_answer: Cyclophoria is the latent heterophoric condition in which the eyes exhibit torsional (rotational) deviation when normal binocular visual stimuli that maintain alignment are removed.

256957.long_answer: The disorder is Grover disease, also called transient acantholytic dermatosis. It was first described in 1975 by American dermatopathologist Dr. Ralph W. Grover. Histologically, Grover disease shows focal acantholysis—the loss of intercellular desmosomal connections between keratinocytes—exactly the feature seen in pemphigus vulgaris and notably absent in bullous pemphigoid, making this microscopic finding a key diagnostic clue.

619420.long_answer: Babesia species (babesiosis) produce intra-erythrocytic tetrads that form the characteristic “Maltese cross,” named after the cross used by Crusaders. On peripheral blood smear these ring forms closely mimic those of Plasmodium species. Because both infections involve protozoa invading red blood cells and can cause febrile hemolytic illness, the foremost condition that must be distinguished from babesiosis is malaria caused by Plasmodium spp.; hence, malaria is the primary differential diagnosis.

845857.long_answer: Andersen disease (glycogen-storage disease type IV) is caused by deficiency of the glycogen-branching enzyme, amylo-1,4→1,6-transglucosidase (EC 2.4.1.18). This enzyme catalyzes transfer of a segment of a 1,4-α-glucan chain to form 1,6-α branches in glycogen. Because it mediates transfer of glycosyl groups from one molecule site to another, it is classified in the ‘transferase’ family of enzymes (specifically, among glycosyltransferases).

921794.long_answer: The condition is precocious puberty. In 1852, Dr. Robert King Stone—who later became President Abraham Lincoln’s personal physician—published the first detailed medical report of a boy with markedly premature sexual development, introducing the entity now termed precocious puberty. The disorder is defined by the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics and other pubertal changes well before the normal age threshold (before 9 years in boys), and it remains the classic medical condition associated with abnormally early-onset puberty in young males.

857333.long_answer: Jens Christian Skou first described the sodium-potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) in 1957. This membrane transporter hydrolyses ATP to exchange intracellular Na⁺ for extracellular K⁺ and therefore depends critically on an adequate ATP supply. In Hashimoto’s encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis), autoantibodies directed against α-enolase interfere with glycolysis, reducing cellular ATP production. With diminished ATP, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is one of the first ion transporters to fail, leading to neuronal ionic imbalance and contributing to the encephalopathic manifestations of the disorder.

656674.long_answer: In Joubert syndrome the eyelid drooping (ptosis) is attributed to weakness or dysfunction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, the striated muscle that normally lifts the upper eyelid. Impairment of this muscle prevents adequate eyelid elevation, producing the characteristic ptosis seen in affected patients.

666822.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is a mosaic over-growth disorder caused by activating AKT1 mutations. In addition to over-growth of bone, soft tissue, and skin, patients have an elevated risk of several neoplasms. In males, the main reproductive-system malignancy reported is testicular cancer—most often seminomatous or other germ-cell tumors. Multiple clinical series and reviews of Proteus syndrome list testicular carcinoma among the tumors occurring with increased frequency, making it the primary reproductive cancer risk for affected male patients.

731031.long_answer: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that shuttles electrons between complexes I/II and III in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. Humans synthesize CoQ10 endogenously, and additional amounts are obtained from dietary sources such as oily fish, meat, and nuts. Supplemental CoQ10 has been shown in controlled clinical studies to improve myocardial energy production, reduce oxidative stress, and enhance ejection fraction in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, thereby helping to treat the resultant heart failure.

278085.long_answer: Bardet-Biedl syndrome is genetically heterogeneous, with each causative gene defining a numbered subtype of the disorder. Pathogenic variants in the BBS1 gene cause the phenotype classified as Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 1 (BBS1). Hence, mutations in the BBS1 gene are specifically associated with BBS type 1.

155398.long_answer: In children, the condition most frequently linked to Fanconi syndrome is cystinosis. Cystinosis results from loss-of-function mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter cystinosin. Defects in CTNS cause cystine accumulation in lysosomes, leading to the proximal renal tubular dysfunction characteristic of Fanconi syndrome.

893226.long_answer: Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) routinely prescribed for chronic inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis. Clinical and public-health guidelines for symptomatic management of Chikungunya advise the use of NSAIDs—after dengue has been excluded—to control the high fever, arthralgia, and joint edema characteristic of the infection. Among the recommended options, naproxen is specifically mentioned because of its established anti-inflammatory and antipyretic efficacy. Thus, naproxen is the NSAID of choice for relieving fever and joint swelling in patients with Chikungunya.

151378.long_answer: The cerebral cortex is the expansive outer layer of the cerebrum and constitutes the largest site of neural integration in the central nervous system, processing and integrating sensory, motor, and associative information. Epileptic seizures arise when cortical neurons exhibit synchronous, excessive, and abnormal electrical discharges; thus, the cerebral cortex is the primary brain region implicated in the generation of epileptic activity.

728397.long_answer: Hypochondriasis (now termed illness-anxiety disorder) often responds to the same medications used for depressive and anxiety disorders. Several controlled trials and clinical reports have shown that SSRIs—such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, and fluvoxamine—significantly lessen preoccupation with somatic illness, decrease health-related anxiety, and improve overall functioning. Because SSRIs are first-line antidepressants for major depressive disorder and have established efficacy and safety profiles, they are the drug class most commonly prescribed to reduce hypochondriacal symptoms.

234430.long_answer: The acute confusional state that can arise within hours to days after exposure to mefloquine (or related quinoline antimalarials) is medically termed delirium. Delirium is a fluctuating disturbance of consciousness and cognition often accompanied by hallucinations, agitation, and disorientation. In cases of mefloquine-induced chronic encephalopathy, delirium is recognized as one of the cardinal, early neuropsychiatric manifestations and is sometimes misinterpreted as post-traumatic stress disorder because of overlapping symptoms such as anxiety, hyperarousal, and intrusive experiences.

655589.long_answer: Paragonimiasis is the tissue-fluke infection produced by Paragonimus species (most often Paragonimus westermani). Although the adult worms characteristically lodge in the lungs, aberrant migration occurs in a substantial proportion of patients. Epidemiologic series show that 10 – 24 % of documented Paragonimus infections involve ectopic sites, most commonly the brain or spinal cord, giving rise to cerebral (neurologic) paragonimiasis. When the parasite lodges in the central nervous system it can provoke seizures, focal deficits, intracranial inflammation and, on occasion, thrombotic complications such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – a rare form of stroke produced by clotting of the brain’s dural venous sinuses. Therefore, the parasitic disease whose central-nervous-system involvement is seen in roughly 10–24 % of affected individuals and is linked to CVST is paragonimiasis.

524762.long_answer: Pediatric (X-linked) gigantism is produced by micro-duplications in the Xq26.3 locus that include the GPR101 gene, while Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome is caused by loss-of-function changes in the neighbouring GPC3/GPC4 locus in Xq26.2. Thus, the shared chromosomal region implicated in both disorders is the long-arm segment Xq26 of the X chromosome.

679390.long_answer: Deferiprone (brand name Ferriprox) is an oral iron-chelating agent. It received its first marketing authorization from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 1999 for the treatment of iron overload in patients with thalassemia major. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval 12 years later, in 2011. Because deferiprone removes excess iron from the body, it is also employed in managing iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis when standard phlebotomy is unsuitable. Thus, deferiprone fits the description of a medication approved by the FDA for thalassemia major 12 years after EMA approval and also used to treat hemochromatosis.

829837.long_answer: The triad of gait instability, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence defines normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). The standard first-line management for NPH is surgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid with a ventriculoperitoneal (or equivalent CSF) shunt, which can substantially improve gait, cognition, and bladder control.

638322.long_answer: The thread-like nematode genus in question is Gongylonema, first erected by Giovanni Battista Molin in 1857. Species of Gongylonema are important parasites of many domestic animals (e.g., cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry) and only rarely infect humans (causing the uncommon disease gongylonemiasis). Taxonomically, Gongylonema belongs to the family Gongylonematidae, which is placed within the suborder Spirurina of the class Chromadorea. Hence, the suborder of Chromadorea that encompasses this genus—and therefore fits the description given—is Spirurina.

649969.long_answer: The progeroid cutis laxa (De Barsy) syndrome that presents with a prematurely aged appearance, generalized cutis laxa, growth and developmental delay, and characteristic ocular findings such as bilateral corneal clouding is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ALDH18A1 gene. ALDH18A1 encodes Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS); deficiency of this enzyme disrupts proline and ornithine biosynthesis, leading to the connective-tissue and ocular abnormalities that define the syndrome.

683309.long_answer: In angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), the reactive B-cell population is very often infected by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). The prototypical and most common disease caused by EBV is infectious mononucleosis (“mono,” glandular fever). Thus, the virus present in the B-cells of AITL is the same agent that commonly produces infectious mononucleosis.

651642.long_answer: Arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene (or the related VIPAS39). VPS33B encodes a member of the Sec1/Munc18 family that forms part of the class C Vps tethering complex. This protein regulates the docking and fusion of intracellular transport vesicles with their target membranes, thereby ensuring correct trafficking of proteins to apical, endosomal and lysosomal compartments. In other words, the gene mediates vesicle-mediated protein sorting within the cell.

414459.long_answer: Gliosarcoma is a rare malignant brain tumor that the 2007 World Health Organization (WHO) classification lists as a histologic subtype (variant) of glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumor. Epidemiologic data compiled by the U.S. National Cancer Institute’s SEER program show that patients with gliosarcoma have an exceptionally poor prognosis, with a reported five-year relative survival rate of about 5.6 %. These features—rarity, classification under glioblastoma in the 2007 WHO system, and the specific 5.6 % five-year survival figure—identify gliosarcoma as the tumor described in the question.

170150.long_answer: Autosomal‐recessive primary microcephaly is most frequently caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ASPM gene (abnormal spindle-like, microcephaly-associated). ASPM is located on chromosome 1q31, and defective alleles lead to markedly reduced brain size and the characteristic congenital microcephaly phenotype.

558304.long_answer: MPI-CDG (Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation type Ib) is caused by pathogenic variants in the MPI gene, which encodes the human phosphomannose isomerase enzyme. The canonical human phosphomannose isomerase protein (UniProt accession P34949) is composed of 406 amino acid residues. Therefore, the enzyme whose mutations lead to MPI-CDG contains 406 amino acid residues.

450226.long_answer: Mulibrey nanism—often referred to as the muscle-liver-brain-eye (Mulibrey) growth-delay syndrome—is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by severe pre- and post-natal growth retardation, typical craniofacial features and multiorgan involvement. Comprehensive genetic studies have shown that every confirmed case of Mulibrey nanism carries biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the gene TRIM37, located on chromosome 17q22–q23. No other gene has been implicated in this specific growth-delay syndrome, making TRIM37 the definitive causal gene.

254228.long_answer: Severe, generalized accumulation of fluid in the subcutaneous tissues and serous cavities is termed anasarca. In diabetic nephropathy, heavy proteinuria and subsequent hypoalbuminemia lower plasma oncotic pressure, leading to marked, body-wide edema—clinically described as anasarca.

954659.long_answer: Trichothiodystrophy manifests with brittle hair, ichthyotic skin, nail abnormalities, and neurologic deficits—all structures that originate from the embryonic ectoderm. Because the disorder predominantly involves these ectoderm-derived tissues, it is considered an ectodermal dysplasia.

663367.long_answer: The slogan “The Other White Meat” was created by the U.S. National Pork Board to market pork as a lean alternative comparable to poultry. Despite this positioning, pork is still classified as red meat and contains appreciable amounts of saturated fat. Diets high in saturated fat can raise serum LDL-cholesterol levels and contribute to secondary (diet-induced) hyperlipidemia. Therefore, pork—the meat promoted as 'the other white meat'—is also implicated in causing secondary hyperlipidemia through its saturated-fat content.

254319.long_answer: Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) contains potent cardiac glycosides that make all parts of the plant highly toxic if ingested. Despite this toxicity, gardeners frequently cultivate it as a biennial—sowing seed one year for flowering the next—because of its tall spikes densely packed with vivid purple, pink, or white tubular flowers that add striking color to ornamental beds and borders.

157829.long_answer: The standard over-the-counter topical medication used to relieve pruritus (itching) from contact dermatitis caused by Toxicodendron species—such as poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac—is calamine lotion. Calamine is a pink-colored preparation made from a finely powdered mineral mixture of zinc oxide with a small proportion of ferric oxide, suspended in a water-based lotion. When applied to the affected skin, it provides a cooling, antipruritic, and mildly astringent effect, thereby reducing itch and discomfort associated with the rash.

684640.long_answer: The described disorder is Bloom syndrome, an autosomal-recessive condition especially frequent in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. It presents with marked pre- and postnatal growth deficiency (short stature), photosensitive skin changes, genomic instability leading to a greatly elevated risk of a broad spectrum of cancers, and features that can resemble premature aging. Bloom syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the BLM gene on chromosome 15q26.1, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase crucial for DNA repair and genomic stability. Identification of pathogenic variants in BLM confirms the diagnosis.

796862.long_answer: Although the condition is now called Lynch syndrome after the later work of Henry T. Lynch, the first physician to recognize and describe this inherited predisposition to colorectal (and other) cancers was pathologist Aldred Scott Warthin. In 1913 he published observations on “Family G,” documenting an autosomal-dominant pattern of early-onset colon and endometrial cancers, thereby identifying the hereditary cancer syndrome that would decades later be renamed Lynch syndrome.

753323.long_answer: The most prevalent form of arthritis is osteoarthritis. Synovial fluid from an osteoarthritic joint is classified as “non-inflammatory”: it remains clear (transparent) and shows only a slight straw-yellow tint. This clear, lightly yellow appearance helps distinguish it from the turbid, more intensely colored fluid seen in inflammatory or infectious arthritides.

232559.long_answer: The condition is HIV-associated eosinophilic folliculitis.  It presents with intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and pustules centered on hair follicles, most often on the face, scalp, neck, upper chest and back.  The lesions appear in patients with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease, typically when CD4 counts are low.
