HIV is a member of the lentivirus genus, so the eruption is ultimately caused by infection with a lentivirus and is therefore tightly linked to advanced HIV/AIDS.

253003.long_answer: Deferiprone is an orally active iron-chelating agent (marketed as Ferriprox) that received its first marketing authorisation in the European Union in August 1999 for the treatment of transfusional iron overload in patients with thalassaemia major. Because it can be taken by mouth and effectively lowers body iron stores, deferiprone is also employed in patients with hereditary haemochromatosis who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to regular phlebotomy, providing an alternative means of reducing excess iron.

244933.long_answer: The TP53 gene (commonly referred to as p53) is a classic tumor-suppressor gene situated at chromosome 17p13.1—the short (p) arm of chromosome 17. Its genomic locus spans roughly 20 kilobases. Loss-of-function mutations or deletions of TP53 are frequently documented in malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs), contributing to defective cell-cycle control and genomic instability characteristic of these aggressive sarcomas.

665260.long_answer: The chromosomal disorder Down syndrome (trisomy 21), first described by the physician John Langdon Down, markedly increases the likelihood of developing acute myeloid leukemia—especially the megakaryoblastic (AML-M7) subtype. Children with Down syndrome have a several-hundred–fold higher incidence of AML compared with the general population, making this congenital condition a well-recognized risk factor for the disease.

129442.long_answer: Follicular lymphoma (FL) occasionally undergoes ‘histologic transformation’ to an aggressive form of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Molecular studies and pathologic series have shown that the acquisition of latent infection by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is a recognized driver of this transformation. The virus’s latent proteins (e.g., LMP1, EBNA2) activate NF-κB and other growth-promoting pathways, fostering the aggressive phenotype characteristic of DLBCL. Hence, EBV is the viral agent implicated in the progression of follicular lymphoma to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

960525.long_answer: Petrolatum (commonly called petroleum jelly or white petrolatum) is an occlusive barrier whose melting point generally falls between 40 °C and 70 °C. It is widely recommended in dermatology for managing xeroderma because it forms an impermeable film that reduces transepidermal water loss. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration lists petrolatum as an approved over-the-counter skin protectant active ingredient, confirming its recognized safety and effectiveness for this purpose.

582369.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the BCOR (BCL6 corepressor) gene are known to cause the X-linked form of syndromic microphthalmia that OMIM designates as Microphthalmia, Syndromic 2 (MCOPS2), also called oculofaciocardiodental/Lenz microphthalmia syndrome.

329502.long_answer: The rare genetic disorder linked to an extra copy of DNA on the long (q) arm of chromosome 15 is called Dup15q syndrome, also known as chromosome 15q11-q13 duplication syndrome or isodicentric 15 syndrome. In this condition, individuals carry an additional duplicated segment (either interstitial or as an isodicentric supernumerary chromosome) involving 15q11.2-q13. The dosage increase of genes within this region disrupts neurodevelopment, leading to features such as hypotonia, developmental delay, seizures, autism spectrum behaviors, and varying degrees of intellectual disability. Thus, duplication of 15q material underlies the intellectual impairment characteristic of Dup15q syndrome.

525642.long_answer: Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (the phenotype seen in pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a) is classically associated with sensorineural deafness, mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, and characteristic skeletal abnormalities such as short 4th/5th metacarpals and metatarsals, brachydactyly, and other malformations of the bones of the fingers and toes.

143907.long_answer: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a group of inherited metabolic disorders caused by deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This enzyme defect blocks the normal catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Accumulation of these amino acids and their toxic ketoacids leads to neonatal encephalopathy that frequently presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and generalized hypotonia. Accordingly, MSUD is listed among the principal inborn errors of metabolism that can cause hypotonia in newborns.

430378.long_answer: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—agents such as ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin, and other COX inhibitors—are widely used for analgesia and to control inflammation. By inhibiting renal prostaglandin synthesis, they reduce renin release and aldosterone secretion, impair renal potassium excretion, and can precipitate hyperkalemia, especially in patients with renal impairment or those taking other potassium-raising drugs.

799512.long_answer: The congenital condition is bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). BAV is the most common congenital heart defect, occurring in about 1–2 % of the population. Beyond causing valvular dysfunction, BAV is well known for its association with dilatation of the ascending aorta—the largest artery in the body—due to intrinsic aortopathy and altered hemodynamics. Therefore, bicuspid aortic valve is the condition linked to aortic dilatation.

437386.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies have consistently shown that men with diabetes mellitus experience markedly higher rates of erectile dysfunction (impotence) than men without diabetes. Large population-based analyses indicate that the prevalence of erectile dysfunction in diabetic men is approximately 3.5 times greater than in nondiabetic men, largely because chronic hyperglycemia accelerates vascular and neuropathic damage that impairs penile blood flow and nitric-oxide–mediated smooth-muscle relaxation. Therefore, the sexual dysfunction that is 3.5 times more common in men with diabetes mellitus is erectile dysfunction.

352067.long_answer: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is an autosomal-recessive disorder that can result from mutations in more than 40 different genes encoding components of motile cilia (e.g., DNAH5, DNAI1, CCDC39, CCDC40). Defective ciliary structure or function impairs mucociliary clearance throughout the respiratory tract, leading to chronic sinusitis, recurrent otitis media, and persistent lower-airway infections such as bronchiectasis. The hallmark pathophysiology is abnormal mucociliary clearance, which explains the lifelong pattern of chronic respiratory infections seen in affected individuals.

632138.long_answer: Ocular toxoplasmosis, caused by infection with the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii, is the classic infectious cause of chorioretinitis. It produces focal necrotizing lesions in the retina and choroid, and patients most often present with painless, unilateral loss of vision or blurred vision—a decrease in visual acuity in one eye. This presentation makes toxoplasmosis the prototypical infectious etiology of chorioretinitis described in ophthalmology and infectious-disease texts.

921534.long_answer: In the 2016 (and current) World Health Organization classification, acute myeloid leukemia—including the minimally differentiated (M0) subtype—is diagnosed only when blast cells constitute at least 20 % of nucleated cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood, provided that none of the defining recurrent genetic abnormalities (which would allow a lower blast count) are present.

423479.long_answer: Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) is produced by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase, commonly called arylsulfatase B (ARSB). X-ray crystallographic analysis of human ARSB (e.g., PDB entry 1FSU) shows that its polypeptide chain folds into a canonical arylsulfatase α/β-fold composed of a central eight-stranded β-sheet surrounded by 17 distinct α-helices. Thus, the secondary-structure of the enzyme contains seventeen α-helices.

749466.long_answer: Balderdash syndrome is an early colloquial name for the psychiatric condition now called Ganser syndrome, characterized by the giving of approximate or nonsensical answers. The disorder was first described in 1898 by the German psychiatrist Sigbert Josef Maria Ganser (1853–1931) while he was working with prisoners in a Hamburg jail. Because of his seminal description, the condition bears his surname, and he is the physician remembered for this eponymous, or “balderdash,” syndrome.

854124.long_answer: Hematopoiesis (also spelled haemopoiesis) is the fundamental physiological process by which all new blood cellular elements—erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets—are continuously produced from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. This process takes place primarily in the bone marrow, the tissue that is commonly biopsied in suspected Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) to look for characteristic macrophage (histiocyte) infiltration and hemophagocytosis. Thus, hematopoiesis is the key process occurring in the bone marrow that generates new blood cells.

222137.long_answer: The disease described is hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa). Severity of this chronic inflammatory skin condition is routinely classified using the three-tier Hurley staging system: Stage I (single or multiple abscesses without sinus tracts), Stage II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tract formation and scarring, widely separated), and Stage III (diffuse or interconnected sinus tracts and abscesses across a region). This classification guides treatment decisions, including the use of biologic agents such as the TNF-α inhibitor infliximab for moderate-to-severe disease.

795817.long_answer: The described condition is the Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon, a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis. In this anomaly, voluntary movements of the jaw (chewing, opening, lateral excursion) produce an involuntary, rhythmic elevation of the upper eyelid. It results from aberrant connections between branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and the oculomotor nerve that innervates the levator palpebrae superioris. Clinically, it is seen as ptosis at rest with a sudden ‘wink’—an upward jerk of the eyelid—whenever the jaw moves, fitting the description given.

490774.long_answer: The human F2 gene encodes coagulation factor II, commonly known as prothrombin. Prothrombin is the zymogen precursor that is proteolytically cleaved to generate the active serine protease thrombin, a central enzyme in the coagulation cascade responsible for converting fibrinogen to fibrin and activating several other clotting factors. Extensive genetic, biochemical and clinical studies have firmly established that mutations in the F2 gene alter prothrombin levels or function, leading to bleeding disorders or thrombophilia, confirming that F2 specifically encodes prothrombin (coagulation factor II).

707707.long_answer: The disease is pulmonary siderosis, a form of pneumoconiosis that develops after chronic inhalation of fine iron or iron-oxide (rust) dust. These particles are deposited in the lung’s alveoli—the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs—leading to characteristic patchy accumulations of iron visible histologically and radiographically. Although often asymptomatic, this occupational lung disease illustrates the effect of repeated iron dust exposure on pulmonary tissue.

100860.long_answer: The confirmation of complete mirror-image reversal of the heart and visceral organs in situs inversus totalis is typically obtained with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI produces detailed cross-sectional images without using ionizing radiation and has even been applied to the study of ancient mummies, making it a suitable non-ionizing modality for both archaeological imaging and modern clinical assessment of organ position.

838174.long_answer: Seizures that can accompany encephalitis are commonly managed with anticonvulsant (antiepileptic) drugs. This heterogeneous class of agents—including medications such as phenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate and others—acts by stabilizing neuronal membranes and inhibiting the excessive, rapid firing of neurons that underlies seizure activity. Their shared ability to dampen aberrant neuronal excitability makes anticonvulsants the standard pharmacological approach for seizure control in encephalitis patients.

483615.long_answer: Blue-cone monochromacy involves the two highly homologous X-linked cone-opsin genes, OPN1LW (long-wave/red) and OPN1MW (medium-wave/green).  Across their coding regions these genes are almost identical, but they differ in a set of fixed, gene-specific nucleotide positions—commonly termed dimorphic (or “dismorphic”) sites.  Comparative sequencing has shown that there are 15 such dimorphic sites, which account for all of the consistent amino-acid differences between the L- and M-cone pigments.  Hence, the two homologous genes differ at 15 dimorphic sites.

901282.long_answer: The eponym “Marie–Strümpell disease” for ankylosing spondylitis arises from the work of two neurologists: the German neurologist Adolph von Strümpell and the French neurologist Pierre Marie. Strümpell had earlier, in 1880, provided the first description of hereditary spastic paraplegia, hence the alternative name “Strümpell-Lorrain disease.” In the same year (1880) Strümpell and Pierre Marie published descriptions of the inflammatory spinal disorder now called ankylosing spondylitis. Because Strümpell is already identified in the question as the first describer of hereditary spastic paraplegia, the other neurologist who shared credit for describing ankylosing spondylitis is Pierre Marie.

505048.long_answer: Ocrelizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 antigen on B-lymphocytes. It is approved for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and, because B-cell depletion is also beneficial in autoimmune blistering diseases, ocrelizumab is currently being investigated as a potential therapy for pemphigus vulgaris.

412427.long_answer: In hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, multiple arteriovenous malformations create low-resistance shunts that divert blood away from capillary beds. This reduces effective organ perfusion. To maintain adequate systemic perfusion and blood pressure, the heart compensates by pumping a larger volume of blood per minute—i.e., it increases its cardiac output (via higher heart rate and/or stroke volume). This sustained elevation in cardiac output characterizes the high-output state often seen in patients with extensive AV malformations.

502680.long_answer: Activated protein C (APC) resistance in hereditary thrombophilia is most commonly caused by the Factor V Leiden mutation, a single-nucleotide substitution in the F5 gene. The F5 (coagulation factor V) gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 1 at position 1q23. Therefore, the gene mutated in the prevalent hereditary form of APC resistance resides on chromosome 1.

715914.long_answer: The PEPD gene encodes prolidase, an enzyme required to recycle proline and hydroxyproline released during collagen turnover. When PEPD is mutated, prolidase activity is lost, collagen degradation and resynthesis are disrupted, and the composition and organization of the extracellular matrix (the fibrous network that supports all connective tissues) become abnormal. This defective extracellular matrix underlies the skin lesions, poor wound healing, and other connective-tissue manifestations seen in prolidase (PEPD) deficiency.

151952.long_answer: Infliximab is a chimeric (mouse-human) IgG1 monoclonal antibody that specifically binds to tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and neutralizes its biological activity. Although primarily approved for Crohn’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory disorders, infliximab has been used off-label to treat refractory cases of collagenous colitis, taking advantage of its TNF-α–blocking action to reduce mucosal inflammation.

571170.long_answer: The AI variant that shows characteristically enlarged (taurodont) pulp chambers and an apically displaced furcation is the hypomaturation–hypoplastic type associated with taurodontism, traditionally classified as Type IV amelogenesis imperfecta.

103768.long_answer: The disorder is Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD).  In DSM-5, BDD is grouped with the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.  Its hallmark is an intense, time-consuming preoccupation with an imagined or greatly exaggerated defect in physical appearance—typically focused on skin, hair, nose, or other body parts—and this concern is explicitly unrelated to body weight or shape.  This distinguishes BDD from anorexia nervosa, an eating disorder characterized by fear of weight gain and restrictive eating behaviors aimed at lowering body weight.  Thus, BDD is the contrasting obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorder sought in the question.

149439.long_answer: Syphilitic leukoplakia is an oral white patch that appears during tertiary syphilis. The causative organism of syphilis is Treponema pallidum, a slender, spiral-shaped spirochete that is microaerophilic and classified with gram-negative bacteria because it possesses a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide-like molecules. Persistent infection of oral tissues by Treponema pallidum produces the characteristic leukoplakic lesion, hence the name syphilitic leukoplakia.

947220.long_answer: The condition is neonatal (physiologic) jaundice, a common, usually benign yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera caused by elevated serum bilirubin. It appears in about 80 % of newborns during their first week of life because their hepatic bilirubin-conjugating mechanisms are immature and bilirubin production from hemoglobin breakdown is high. Levels peak around days 3–5 and then fall as liver function matures.

655782.long_answer: The lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase is Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA (Morquio A syndrome). In February 2014, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the enzyme-replacement therapy elosulfase alfa (marketed as Vimizim) specifically for the treatment of this condition, providing patients with a recombinant form of the missing enzyme.

687426.long_answer: Michels syndrome is a craniosynostosis-containing malformation syndrome in which the premature fusion occurs at the coronal sutures—the paired fibrous joints that run transversely between the frontal and parietal bones of the skull. Early closure of these sutures produces the brachycephalic skull shape and associated mid-face and orbital findings characteristic of the disorder.

442504.long_answer: In Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, involvement of the cardiac conduction system often leads to sinus node dysfunction. This manifests as sinus bradycardia, defined as a resting heart rate of fewer than 60 beats per minute. Sinus bradycardia is well documented in patients with this muscular dystrophy alongside other conduction disturbances such as atrioventricular block and atrial arrhythmias.

643490.long_answer: In the autosomal-recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophies caused by loss of any sarcoglycan (α, β, γ or δ)—classified as LGMD 2C, 2D, 2E and 2F—absence of the sarcoglycan subunit destabilises the entire dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. This secondary destabilisation can lead to a reduced or patchy dystrophin signal on immunohistochemistry even though the dystrophin gene itself is intact. Therefore, the sarcoglycan-deficient limb-girdle muscular dystrophies are the forms that may show decreased dystrophin staining without dystrophin mutations.

363368.long_answer: PCDH7 (protocadherin-7) belongs to the protocadherin subfamily within the cadherin superfamily of calcium-dependent cell-adhesion molecules. Genetic mapping and sequencing studies of patients with congenital tracheoesophageal malformations have identified variants in PCDH7, and the gene has therefore been put forward as a candidate gene for esophageal atresia. Its involvement is biologically plausible because protocadherins participate in epithelial cell-cell adhesion processes that are essential for correct foregut septation during embryonic development, the step that fails in esophageal atresia.

466063.long_answer: Immunoglobulin E (IgE) is the scarcest immunoglobulin isotype in normal serum, circulating at concentrations far lower than IgG, IgA, IgM, or IgD. Despite its low abundance, IgE binds with high affinity to Fcε receptors on mast cells and basophils, priming them for immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a severe, recurrent allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva in which elevated local and systemic IgE levels, together with IgE-sensitized mast cells, drive the release of histamine and other mediators that produce itching, photophobia, and conjunctival papillae. Therefore, IgE is the immunoglobulin implicated in vernal keratoconjunctivitis and is also the least abundant isotype in the bloodstream.

636294.long_answer: The major plasma protein produced by the yolk sac and frequently elevated in hepatoblastomas is alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). The human AFP gene encodes a precursor polypeptide that is 609 amino acids long (UniProt P02771). After removal of its 18-residue signal peptide, the mature secreted protein comprises residues 19–609, but the total length of the encoded polypeptide is 609 amino acids.

593161.long_answer: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—the first-line pharmacologic treatment for active axial spondyloarthritis—work by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and thereby reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Renal prostaglandins normally help maintain adequate renal blood flow, especially under conditions of decreased effective circulating volume. By lowering prostaglandin levels, NSAIDs can constrict the afferent arteriole and diminish renal perfusion, increasing the risk of acute kidney injury or worsening chronic kidney disease. This renal safety concern is well documented for commonly used agents such as naproxen, ibuprofen, indomethacin, diclofenac and celecoxib, all of which are considered first-line options in axial spondyloarthritis management.

928221.long_answer: In their 1989 report on dynamic smile reconstruction in children with Möbius syndrome, Zuker and colleagues described using a free gracilis muscle transfer innervated by the motor branch of the trigeminal nerve that supplies the masseter. They proposed the masseteric nerve as the donor because it is reliably present and strong in these patients even when the facial (VII) nerve is absent or non-functional. Coapting the gracilis motor nerve to the masseteric nerve restored voluntary contraction of the transplanted muscle and allowed the children to regain the ability to smile.

575067.long_answer: Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase. The recombinant, commercially available form of this enzyme—used for enzyme-replacement therapy in affected patients—is laronidase, marketed under the trade name Aldurazyme.

827382.long_answer: Levodopa, usually administered in combination with the peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa, is the standard medication for dopamine-responsive dystonia. The same levodopa/carbidopa regimen is also a cornerstone of therapy for the autosomal recessive form of GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency because it replaces the dopamine that cannot be synthesized adequately in both conditions.

666699.long_answer: In Angle’s classification, a Class III malocclusion is characterized by mandibular prognathism: the lower dental arch and incisors lie anterior to the upper dental arch, producing an ‘under-bite.’ This relationship results from an excessively protruding lower jaw or a retrusive maxilla, causing the lower teeth to occlude ahead of the upper teeth.

947752.long_answer: During embryonic folding, the lateral plate mesoderm splits into a somatic (parietal) layer, which associates with surface ectoderm to form the ventral body wall, and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, which covers the gut tube. Proper fusion of the somatic/parietal layers from the right and left sides is essential to close the anterior thoracic wall. Failure of this parietal layer to develop or fuse correctly leaves a midline defect through which the heart protrudes, producing ectopia cordis. Hence, defective formation of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm underlies ectopia cordis.

830404.long_answer: Mutations in the Indian hedgehog (IHH) gene—an essential component of the Hedgehog signaling pathway—cause the congenital skeletal disorder known as Brachydactyly type A1. Affected individuals are born with abnormally short fingers and/or toes because the middle phalanges fail to develop properly. Thus, Brachydactyly type A1 is the congenital syndrome linked directly to Hedgehog pathway dysfunction.

512370.long_answer: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (idiopathic brachial neuritis) and hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy characteristically injure branches of the brachial plexus, with the axillary nerve being one of the nerves most often involved. The axillary nerve exclusively supplies the deltoid, a thick, triangular muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder. Consequently, weakness, pain, and atrophy of the deltoid are common clinical findings in both disorders, making the deltoid the muscle most likely to be affected.

685701.long_answer: The FIP1L1–PDGFRA fusion gene and other activating PDGFRA mutations drive a constitutively active PDGFRA tyrosine kinase in hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) and chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL). Imatinib mesylate is a selective BCR-ABL, KIT and PDGFRA/B tyrosine kinase inhibitor that potently inhibits this aberrant PDGFRA activity. Clinical studies have shown dramatic, often complete, hematologic and molecular remissions in patients with HES or CEL harboring FIP1L1-PDGFRA or other PDGFRA mutations when treated with low-dose imatinib (e.g., 100 mg/day). Consequently, imatinib is the standard tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for these conditions.

859400.long_answer: Hymenolepiasis is a helminthiasis—an infection caused by parasitic worms (helminths).  A major collaborative eradication effort directed at a disease in the same category of helminth infections is the Onchocerciasis Control Programme (OCP) in West Africa, jointly organised by the World Health Organization, the World Bank and several partner nations.  This programme, aimed at eradicating onchocerciasis (river blindness), was officially launched in 1974.  Therefore, the year in which the collaborative disease-eradication programme was launched is 1974.

110195.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis belongs to the group of seronegative spondyloarthritides, meaning that characteristic auto-antibodies directed against nuclear antigens (antinuclear antibodies, ANA) are generally absent. This is true both in adult-onset and juvenile-onset disease. Routine laboratory evaluation of children with suspected juvenile ankylosing spondylitis typically shows negativity for ANA, in contrast to conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus or some forms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis where ANA positivity is common. Therefore, the statement that antibodies binding to nuclear contents are usually not present in juvenile ankylosing spondylitis is correct.

131236.long_answer: Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) is the principal circulating inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. When AAT is deficient, unchecked elastase activity degrades elastin and other structural proteins that are critical for connective-tissue integrity in the lung, liver and vascular walls. Several epidemiological studies and case series have reported a higher prevalence of arterial aneurysms—including abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)—in individuals with severe AAT deficiency (e.g., Pi*ZZ genotype) compared with the general population. Experimental work also demonstrates increased aortic elastin fragmentation and dilatation in AAT-deficient animal models. Taken together, the established mechanism (protease–antiprotease imbalance leading to elastin degradation) and supportive clinical data indicate that AAT deficiency does increase susceptibility to AAA formation. Therefore, the effect of AAT deficiency on connective-tissue integrity is considered a risk factor for developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

132747.long_answer: Leydig cell hypoplasia is caused by inactivating mutations of the luteinizing-hormone/chorionic-gonadotropin (LH/CG) receptor that is expressed almost exclusively on fetal and adult Leydig cells. The primary consequence is underdevelopment of Leydig cells and markedly reduced testosterone production. Sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, which line the seminiferous tubules and provide structural and metabolic support for germ cells, do not express the LH/CG receptor and are not the direct cellular target of the mutation. Although the resultant androgen deficiency can secondarily impair spermatogenesis, the disorder does not directly damage or alter the function of Sertoli cells themselves. Therefore, Leydig cell hypoplasia does not directly affect the sustentacular cells in human testes.

143441.long_answer: The question provides no information indicating that individuals with acro-oto-radial syndrome have the specific, documented deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning required by the DSM-5 definition of intellectual disability. Without evidence of those criteria (confirmed impairments in reasoning, problem solving, academic learning, adaptive behavior, and onset during the developmental period), the statement that the syndrome “fulfills the DSM-5 criteria for intellectual disability” cannot be supported. Therefore, based solely on the information given, the claim is not justified.

152701.long_answer: The caloric reflex test is a vestibular function test in which warm or cold water (or air) is introduced into the external ear canal to stimulate the horizontal semicircular canal and elicit vestibulo-ocular reflexes. It is used primarily to assess vestibular integrity and to provoke or quantify nystagmus arising from labyrinthine or brain-stem pathways. Zonular (lamellar) cataract, however, is an opacity of the lens; its diagnosis relies on slit-lamp biomicroscopy or other ophthalmic imaging, not on vestibular stimulation. While the caloric test can help evaluate vestibular causes of nystagmus, it has no diagnostic value for cataract, and nystagmus itself is generally identified clinically without needing caloric irrigation. Therefore, the caloric reflex test cannot be considered an effective diagnostic tool for the combined conditions “zonular cataract and nystagmus.”

154580.long_answer: People with Down syndrome have well-documented immune dysregulation that makes them more prone to recurrent respiratory, ear, and other infections. Clinical guidelines therefore emphasize rapid and appropriate treatment of any infection (e.g., antibiotics for bacterial illnesses, supportive therapy for viral infections). In addition, measures to bolster or compensate for their relatively weak immune responses—such as up-to-date vaccinations, prophylactic therapies in selected cases, adequate nutrition, and regular medical follow-up—are recommended to help prevent infections and improve overall health. Thus, both infection management and immune-supportive care are considered standard components of medical care for individuals with Down syndrome.

167352.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome type A is caused by pathogenic variants in the ERCC8 gene, which is located on chromosome 5q12. In contrast, Cockayne syndrome type B results from pathogenic variants in the ERCC6 gene, situated on chromosome 10q11.23. Because only the type A gene lies on chromosome 5 while the type B gene is on chromosome 10, it is incorrect to state that the genes responsible for both types are located on chromosome 5.

170557.long_answer: The statement is essentially correct. DAX1 (NR0B1) encodes an atypical nuclear receptor that normally acts as a transcriptional repressor of other nuclear receptors, most notably steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1/NR5A1) and LRH-1. Loss-of-function mutations in DAX1 abolish this negative regulatory activity, leading to derepression of SF-1-dependent gene programs during embryogenesis. This dysregulation disturbs the normal differentiation of several endocrine tissues, including the adrenal cortex and the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. In the pituitary, altered SF-1 activity and downstream signalling impair the proper development and function of gonadotrope and corticotrope lineages, contributing to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and other pituitary deficiencies seen in patients with DAX1 mutations. Therefore, saying that mutations in DAX1 cause pituitary developmental problems by disrupting its negative regulation of other nuclear receptors is consistent with the established mechanistic understanding and is not incorrect.

201807.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the KCNJ6 gene (which encodes the G-protein–activated inwardly rectifying potassium channel 2, GIRK2) are known to cause Keppen-Lubinsky syndrome (also called KCNJ6-related disorder). A core, well-documented feature of this condition is marked intrauterine growth restriction that results in significantly reduced weight, length and head circumference already evident at birth. Therefore, the presence of abnormal (typically decreased) growth parameters at birth is indeed a characteristic, indicative finding of the disease caused by KCNJ6 mutations.

207452.long_answer: L-carnitine serves two clinically useful functions in certain inborn errors of metabolism such as propionic acidemia or related organic acidemias. 1) It facilitates mitochondrial β-oxidation by shuttling long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane, thereby supporting cellular energy production. 2) More importantly for propionic acidemia, L-carnitine conjugates with accumulated toxic acyl-CoA intermediates (e.g., propionyl-CoA) to form acyl-carnitines that are water-soluble and can be excreted in the urine. This lowers intracellular propionic acid and related metabolite levels, regenerates free CoA, and helps prevent secondary mitochondrial dysfunction. Consequently, L-carnitine supplementation is a standard adjunctive therapy in managing metabolic crises and chronic treatment of propionic acidemia and similar disorders, confirming that it enhances energy metabolism while mitigating toxic metabolite buildup.

214705.long_answer: Perimyositis refers to inflammation (the “-itis” suffix) of the perimysium, the connective-tissue sheath that surrounds muscle fascicles. Inflammation is the body’s canonical biological response of living vascular connective tissue to harmful stimuli such as pathogens, damaged cells or irritants. Therefore, because perimyositis is precisely an inflammatory process affecting the connective tissue that envelops muscle fibers, it constitutes part of the biological (inflammatory) response of that connective tissue to harmful stimuli.

238212.long_answer: The provided context contains no information indicating that the early symptoms of psittacosis resemble those of an infection with Salmonella enterica Typhi. Without evidence in the context to support such a similarity, the statement cannot be considered factually correct based solely on the given information.

246741.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) is a group of rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by marked underdevelopment and progressive atrophy of the cerebellum and pons. A core clinical feature across nearly all PCH subtypes is profound global developmental delay. Affected children typically display severe hypotonia, poor or absent head control, and marked psychomotor impairment from early infancy. Because of this severity, most children with PCH do not attain fundamental gross-motor milestones such as independent sitting, crawling, or walking; many never achieve even basic head control. Consequently, by the age of two years, it is uncommon for children with PCH to have reached normal gross motor milestones. Therefore, the statement that they generally reach these milestones by age two is not supported by established medical evidence.

259365.long_answer: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD) is well-known for its cardiac involvement, especially conduction-system disease originating in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Sinus-node dysfunction frequently presents as persistent sinus bradycardia—a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute—and may progress to atrioventricular block or other arrhythmias. Because this slow resting heart rate is a recognized part of the EDMD cardiac phenotype, stating that a resting heart rate of <60 bpm is one of its cardiac manifestations is accurate, not incorrect.

273077.long_answer: Meningococcemia (blood-borne infection with Neisseria meningitidis) frequently co-exists with, or rapidly progresses to, meningococcal meningitis. When the meninges are inflamed, patients develop nuchal rigidity—pain or marked discomfort when the neck is turned, moved, or flexed. Clinical reviews list neck stiffness/pain as a characteristic feature when meningitis accompanies meningococcemia; a substantial proportion of patients with meningococcemia (≈30–50 %) manifest meningeal involvement. Therefore, while isolated septicemia may not cause neck pain, the combined clinical entity “meningococcal disease” (meningococcemia ± meningitis) does include neck discomfort on movement as a recognized symptom.

287953.long_answer: The rare autosomal-dominant skin disorder caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene is Darier disease (Darier–White disease). Standard management is primarily medical (topical or systemic retinoids, keratolytics, etc.), but for localized, thick, or refractory papules and plaques, destructive surgical modalities are accepted adjuncts. Dermatology texts and treatment guidelines list electrosurgical techniques—electrodesiccation/electrocoagulation performed with high-frequency, alternating-polarity radio-frequency current—as an option to ablate hypertrophic lesions and achieve hemostasis. Although not curative and reserved for selected areas, this procedure is indeed a recognized treatment approach within the therapeutic armamentarium for Darier disease.

290537.long_answer: Autosomal recessive GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency impairs synthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a co-factor required for the hydroxylation of tyrosine to L-DOPA. Because of the BH4 shortage, patients cannot produce adequate amounts of the catecholamine neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Clinical management therefore includes providing downstream precursors that bypass the defective enzymatic step. Administration of L-DOPA (usually combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa) supplies the immediate precursor of these catecholamines, restores neurotransmitter levels in the central nervous system, and improves the neurologic symptoms of the disorder. Consequently, the catecholamine precursor L-DOPA is an accepted component of therapy for autosomal recessive GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency.

313741.long_answer: James R. Lupski, M.D., Ph.D., currently holds the Cullen Foundation Endowed Chair in Molecular Genetics at Baylor College of Medicine. Together with Dr. Lorraine Potocki, he was the first to delineate the microduplication syndrome now known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome (17p11.2 microduplication) in the mid-1990s. Therefore the statement that the physician who presently occupies the Cullen Endowed Chair at BCM was the first to describe Potocki-Lupski syndrome is factually correct, not incorrect.

348471.long_answer: Neutral lipid storage myopathy (NLSD) is pathologically defined by the excessive accumulation of neutral lipids (primarily triacylglycerol) in skeletal-muscle fibers. Muscle-biopsy specimens show numerous cytoplasmic fat droplets that are readily demonstrable with lipid-specific stains (e.g., Oil Red O) and on ultrastructural examination. For electron microscopy, proper fixation with osmium tetroxide preserves the hydrophobic lipid content, allowing the discrete round lipid droplets to be visualized clearly within the myofiber cytoplasm. Consequently, the presence of intramyocellular neutral-lipid droplets and their detection by electron microscopy after osmium tetroxide treatment are well-established diagnostic features of NLSD. Therefore, the statement accurately reflects current biomedical understanding.

353993.long_answer: Species that have produced hallucinatory intoxication in people on Réunion Island—such as spinefoots (Siganus spp.) and sea chubs (Kyphosus spp.)—are primarily shallow-reef herbivores. They are most commonly encountered on coral or rocky substrates in the first few metres below the surface, generally between about 1 m and 30 m, only occasionally extending to roughly 40–60 m. They are not characteristically or predominately distributed at depths of 50–100 m. Therefore the depth range given in the question does not reflect their typical habitat.

361204.long_answer: The Italian scientist Bartolomeo Gosio first isolated mycophenolic acid, from which the modern immunosuppressant agents mycophenolate mofetil / mycophenolate sodium are derived and widely used in solid-organ transplantation. A well-recognized and relatively frequent adverse effect of these mycophenolate preparations is bone-marrow suppression, manifesting clinically as leukopenia (decreased white-blood-cell count); neutropenia and other cytopenias are routinely monitored for in treated transplant patients. Therefore, a decrease in white blood cells is indeed a common adverse reaction to this drug.

396243.long_answer: Primary (familial) hyperlipidemia refers to lipid abnormalities that stem from inherited defects in lipid-metabolizing genes and are present irrespective of dietary intake. When elevated lipid levels are provoked by modifiable external factors—such as excessive consumption of saturated-fat–rich foods like pork and beef—the condition is classified as a secondary or acquired hyperlipidemia. Therefore, hyperlipidemia attributed to a diet high in pork and beef should not be labeled primary hyperlipidemia.

405579.long_answer: Achondroplasia is an inherited disorder of bone growth presenting with disproportionate short stature, bowing or other deformities of the lower limbs, brachydactyly (short fingers), and ligamentous laxity. The condition results from gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene, which negatively regulates endochondral ossification. Therefore, the clinical features described are indeed caused by an FGFR3 gene mutation.

406222.long_answer: Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI) is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC7A7 gene, which encodes the light-chain subunit (y+LAT1) of the heterodimeric cationic-amino-acid transporter system y+L. This transporter functions as an obligate heterodimer composed of the SLC7A7 light chain non-covalently linked to the heavy-chain subunit 4F2hc/CD98, which is encoded by the SLC3A2 gene. The physical association between SLC7A7 and SLC3A2 is required for correct trafficking to the plasma membrane and for transporter activity. Therefore, the gene responsible for LPI (SLC7A7) directly interacts with the SLC3A2 gene product, making the statement correct.

410810.long_answer: Punctate inner choroiditis (PIC) is classically characterized by multiple small, yellow-white chorioretinal lesions in otherwise healthy, often myopic, young women. A defining feature that helps distinguish PIC from other white-dot syndromes (such as multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis) is the relative absence of inflammatory cells in both the anterior chamber and the vitreous. In other words, significant anterior chamber inflammation or vitritis is typically not present in PIC. Therefore, anterior chamber inflammation and vitritis are not considered hallmark or commonly associated findings with punctate inner choroiditis.

415618.long_answer: Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita (CMTC) is primarily a vascular skin malformation, but ophthalmic involvement has been documented. Published case reports and small series describe patients with CMTC who developed congenital or early-onset glaucoma, which is characterized by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). Although this complication is not present in every CMTC patient, the literature confirms that increased IOP can occur as part of the disorder’s spectrum. Therefore, an increase in intraocular pressure is indeed observed in some individuals diagnosed with CMTC.

421218.long_answer: Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in the LYST (LYSosomal Trafficking regulator) gene. The defect disrupts normal formation, trafficking, and release of lysosome-related organelles, including melanosomes in melanocytes. Because the abnormal, oversized melanosomes cannot be properly processed or transferred to keratinocytes, affected individuals show partial oculocutaneous albinism (light skin, silvery hair, and photophobia). This hypopigmentation reflects an intrinsic defect in the handling—and thus the effective production/distribution—of melanin. Therefore, individuals with Chédiak–Higashi syndrome do indeed have a defect that ultimately impairs melanin production/distribution.

422230.long_answer: The 8363G>A point mutation in the mitochondrial MT-TK gene (encoding tRNALys) is a well-documented cause of multisystem mitochondrial disease that can include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and sensorineural hearing loss. The hearing loss results from irreversible damage to cochlear hair cells and/or auditory neurons produced by the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction. At present there are no disease-modifying or curative therapies that can restore normal mitochondrial tRNALys function or regenerate lost cochlear structures. Management is therefore limited to supportive measures such as hearing aids or cochlear implantation, which improve communication but do not biologically reverse the hearing deficit. Consequently, hearing loss produced by this mutation-associated cardiomyopathy is considered irreversible with current medical technology.

422677.long_answer: The well-established fragile sites on the X chromosome are FRAXA at Xq27.3 (associated with the FMR1 gene and Fragile X syndrome) and FRAXE at Xq28; other, much rarer sites such as FRAXF are mapped to Xq22. A fragile site at Xq27.2 is not part of the recognized catalog of cytogenetically confirmed fragile sites. Therefore, stating that a fragile site is located specifically at Xq27.2 is not supported by the established scientific consensus.

427523.long_answer: Ayazi syndrome (also reported as X-linked intellectual disability, Ayazi type; OMIM 300183) is characterised chiefly by moderate to severe intellectual disability, speech delay, seizures, and distinctive cranio-facial or skeletal features. Published clinical descriptions do not list generalized excess adiposity (obesity) as a core or even a recurrent finding. Therefore, the statement that one of the symptoms of Ayazi syndrome is "excessive body fat that has accumulated to such an extent that it can potentially have negative effects on health" (i.e., obesity) is not supported by the established medical literature.

442105.long_answer: Profuse sweating (hyperhidrosis) is one of the cardinal autonomic manifestations of Shapiro syndrome, accompanying its characteristic paroxysmal hypothermia. In contrast, autoimmune encephalopathy (e.g., Hashimoto’s encephalopathy or antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis) is chiefly characterized by subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms—confusion, seizures, cognitive decline, behavioral change—while autonomic features such as sweating are uncommon and not part of the core clinical picture. Therefore, sweating cannot be considered a common symptom shared by both conditions.

449820.long_answer: There is no established biomedical consensus that the gene responsible for Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome encodes a 400-amino-acid protein whose NH₂-terminus contains a T-domain extended by more than 20 additional amino acids relative to other known T-domains. Published data on the molecular basis of Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome do not support this specific description; in fact, the causative gene has not been definitively shown to produce such a uniquely long T-domain protein. Therefore, the statement is not aligned with current scientific knowledge.

450290.long_answer: Pronaxen is a trade name for naproxen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Chikungunya infection does not have a virus-directed treatment; management focuses on relieving its hallmark symptoms of fever, joint pain and inflammation. After dengue has been ruled out, clinical guidelines recommend NSAIDs such as naproxen for symptomatic control of the arthralgia and myalgia associated with Chikungunya. Therefore, using Pronaxen can be considered effective for reducing pain and inflammation in patients with Chikungunya, though it does not eradicate the virus itself.

453784.long_answer: Reduced resistance of skeletal muscle to passive stretching is the clinical definition of hypotonia. Hypotonia is a well-recognized manifestation of several organic acidemias (e.g., propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric, glutaric acidemia type I), frequently appearing in the neonatal period or during metabolic decompensation. It is attributed to metabolic encephalopathy, hyperammonemia, and other biochemical derangements characteristic of these disorders. Therefore, stating that reduced muscle resistance to stretching is one of the symptoms of organic acidemias is consistent with established medical knowledge; it is not incorrect to argue this.

457983.long_answer: Vitamin A is essential for normal differentiation of epithelial tissues. When the body lacks vitamin A, epithelial cells lose their ability to mature properly and instead become hyper-keratinized, a change clinically referred to as hyperkeratosis or follicular keratosis. This process involves excessive synthesis and deposition of keratin—a scleroprotein—within the affected epithelial layers. The resulting overproduction and accumulation of keratin is a well-documented hallmark of vitamin A deficiency, manifesting in dry, rough skin, keratinised conjunctival plaques (Bitot spots), and other keratinisation disorders. Therefore, the statement that keratin can be overproduced in cases of vitamin A deficiency is consistent with established biomedical knowledge.

473053.long_answer: Grebe-type chondrodysplasia (also called acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type) is a very rare skeletal dysplasia distinguished by marked shortening of the limbs while the trunk is relatively spared. Reported adults with this condition generally reach a stature well below 147 cm (4 ft 10 in), often under 120 cm. Despite the severe skeletal abnormalities, neurological development is normal and no intellectual disability is associated with the disorder. Therefore, the statement that Grebe-type chondrodysplasia typically results in an adult height of less than 147 cm while leaving intelligence unaffected is consistent with the established clinical description of the condition.

479398.long_answer: XX gonadal dysgenesis can occur as part of Perrault syndrome, a rare genetic disorder in which 46,XX females present with streak ovaries (primary ovarian insufficiency) together with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Sensorineural hearing loss typically impairs the ability to discriminate speech, especially when background noise is present. Therefore, a woman with XX gonadal dysgenesis could indeed experience difficulty distinguishing voices in noisy environments.

490477.long_answer: Pruritus (itching) is a well-recognized and frequent feature of mastocytosis because the excessive release of histamine and other mast-cell mediators directly stimulates cutaneous nerve endings. Herpesvirus infections—both herpes simplex and herpes zoster—also commonly produce itching: patients typically report itching or tingling in the prodromal phase and during healing of the vesicular lesions. Therefore, itching is considered a common symptom encountered in both mastocytosis and herpes.

491820.long_answer: Idiopathic juvenile kyphosis is most frequently known as Scheuermann disease. In the classic medical literature, Scheuermann disease has several synonymous designations, one of which is “osteochondritis deformans juvenilis” (sometimes expanded to “osteochondritis deformans juvenilis dorsi”). Therefore, the term osteochondritis deformans juvenilis is indeed commonly used—especially in older or more formal texts—as a synonym for idiopathic juvenile (Scheuermann) kyphosis.

527304.long_answer:
Extensive epidemiologic and experimental evidence shows that exposure to ionizing radiation increases the incidence of several malignancies, including both brain tumors and chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). 

1. Brain cancer: Survivors of therapeutic cranial irradiation for conditions such as tinea capitis or childhood leukemia, as well as atomic-bomb survivors and patients who received high-dose diagnostic/therapeutic radiation to the head, have a clearly elevated risk of primary brain tumours (e.g., gliomas, meningiomas). This association has been consistently reproduced and accepted as causal by authoritative bodies such as the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the U.S. National Academies’ BEIR committees.

2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML): Ionizing radiation is a well-documented leukemogenic agent. Cohorts of atomic-bomb survivors, radiotherapy patients, and occupationally exposed workers show an increased incidence of CML that rises with cumulative radiation dose. CML is one of the classic hematologic malignancies listed among the radiation-induced cancers by the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) and other expert reviews.

Because ionizing radiation is an established, dose-related risk factor for both primary brain cancers and CML, the statement is correct.

556973.long_answer: The only information supplied is that GMS syndrome was reported in 1992. No data are provided about clinical manifestations, functional limitations, or effects on activities of daily living. Because the question cannot be substantiated with the given context alone, the claim that GMS syndrome negatively affects daily living activities is not supported.

576476.long_answer: Surgical management of anorectal malformations is typically staged and includes procedures that can be revised or undone, such as temporary diverting colostomies that are later closed. Even definitive repairs (e.g., posterior sagittal anorectoplasty) can be modified by subsequent corrective or revision surgeries if necessary. Therefore, operations performed for anorectal malformations are not invariably permanent or irreversible; some components are specifically intended to be temporary and others can be revised to improve function.

579497.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (often abbreviated ODD or ODDD) is a genetic syndrome caused most commonly by pathogenic variants in the GJA1 gene. One of its hallmark skeletal manifestations is syndactyly—partial or complete fusion—of the central digits of the hand. The fusion most frequently involves the third and fourth fingers (middle and ring) and/or the fourth and fifth fingers (ring and little). Because the affected digits are joined and may also exhibit camptodactyly, clinodactyly, or shortened phalanges, patients typically experience restricted independent motion, reduced grip dexterity, and other functional limitations of those fingers. Hence, a condition related to ODD syndrome does indeed affect the functioning of the ring and middle fingers.

586813.long_answer: Hydrochlorothiazide, while commonly used to reduce polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, carries class-related diuretic risks such as intravascular volume depletion, prerenal azotemia or acute kidney injury, and electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia, hyponatremia). These events reflect potential adverse effects on renal function, so clinicians must monitor renal parameters and volume status when prescribing the drug in this population.

588303.long_answer: Long-term cutaneous sequelae after toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are not limited to scarring, dyspigmentation, nail changes and ocular problems. Several case series and reports have documented the later appearance of multiple new benign pigmented lesions—including eruptive lentigines and eruptive melanocytic nevi—months to years after recovery from TEN. These lesions are thought to arise because the massive epidermal destruction in TEN is followed by brisk re-epithelialisation with cytokine-driven melanocyte activation and proliferation; the process can result in numerous small, clinically benign pigmented macules or nevi that were not present before the episode. Therefore, eruptive benign pigmented lesions are a recognised, although uncommon, long-term skin complication in TEN survivors.

597726.long_answer: The provided context contains no information indicating that β-catenin is implicated in the pathology of tetra-amelia syndrome. Therefore, based solely on the available context, there is no support for a role of β-catenin in this condition.

599931.long_answer: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy was first identified and described in the early 1950s by the Portuguese neurologist Mário Corino de Andrade. Prof. Andrade carried out his work in Porto, where he spent the bulk of his career at Hospital Geral de Santo António and the University of Porto’s Faculty of Medicine. Although he became an influential figure in Portuguese neurology, there is no record of him founding any of the major bioscience research institutes based in Lisbon (such as the Instituto Gulbenkian de Ciência, the Instituto de Medicina Molecular, or the Champalimaud Foundation). Those institutions were established by other individuals and organizations. Hence, the statement that the neurologist who first described familial amyloid polyneuropathy was a founder of a major Lisbon bioscience institute is not supported by the historical record.

614616.long_answer: Hereditary Non-polyposis Colorectal Cancer (now commonly called Lynch syndrome) was first systematically described by Prof. Henry T. Lynch. In 1992 the American Cancer Society honored Prof. Lynch with a major society award (reported in contemporary ACS and medical-society press releases as the American Cancer Society Distinguished Service Award/Medal of Honor). Thus, the professor who originally characterized HNPCC did receive an American Cancer Society award in 1992, confirming the statement as accurate.

627609.long_answer: Two parts of the statement are incorrect. (1) Yellow fever is not “one of only two” viral-hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) with a vaccine. In addition to yellow fever, licensed or routinely used human vaccines now exist for several other VHFs—e.g., Ebola virus disease (Ervebo, 2019), dengue (Dengvaxia, 2015), Argentine hemorrhagic fever (Candid #1, used since the 1990s in Argentina), and Kyasanur Forest disease in India. Thus yellow fever is not uniquely one of just two VHFs with an available vaccine. (2) While the World Health Organization states that a single dose of the 17D yellow-fever vaccine provides lifelong protection for immunocompetent persons, this does NOT apply to symptomatic HIV-positive individuals. Because the vaccine is live-attenuated, it is contraindicated in patients with advanced or symptomatic HIV infection or severe immunosuppression (typically CD4 < 200 cells/µL); those who are eligible but immunocompromised may mount a weaker response and may require re-vaccination or repeated serologic testing. Therefore the claim that one dose confers lifelong immunity “even in symptomatic HIV-positive individuals” is not supported by current medical consensus.

655317.long_answer: Accidents (unintentional injuries) are the leading cause of death in U.S. children aged 1–14 years, and malignant neoplasms (childhood cancers) are consistently reported by the CDC as the second leading cause in this age group. Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is a congenital over-growth/epigenetic disorder that confers a markedly elevated risk of several embryonal malignancies—most notably Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma—as well as other childhood cancers. Because BWS children have a significantly higher incidence of these malignancies compared with the general pediatric population, the syndrome is recognized as a cancer‐predisposition condition. Therefore, BWS does increase the risk of the disease category that constitutes the second leading cause of death among U.S. children aged 1–14 years.

666402.long_answer: Parastremmatic dwarfism is classified among the TRPV4-related skeletal dysplasias.  The cardinal pathological features are profound abnormalities of bone development: marked shortening and bowing of the long bones, platyspondyly, kyphoscoliosis, and characteristic dense, striated metaphyseal bone on radiographs.  Although some individuals may have limited range of motion because of the bony deformities themselves, generalized soft-tissue contractures (shortening of muscles, tendons, skin and surrounding soft tissues) are not considered a defining or major component of the disorder.  Such contractures are hallmarks of conditions like arthrogryposis, not parastremmatic dwarfism.  Therefore, the statement that soft-tissue shortening leading to joint stiffness is a major aspect of parastremmatic dwarfism is incorrect.

680746.long_answer: Gonadal agenesis (absence or failure of development of the ovaries or testes) results in very low or absent sex-steroid secretion. In individuals with an XX or XY karyotype who have streak or absent gonads, the Müllerian ducts may form a uterus and upper vagina during fetal life, but post-pubertal growth of the genital tract is estrogen-dependent. Because estrogen is largely absent in gonadal agenesis, the vagina remains infantile—narrow and shorter than normal—and the uterus is small or rudimentary. Therefore, a shortened (hypoplastic) vagina is a recognized consequence of gonadal agenesis, making an anatomic link between the two conditions biologically plausible and documented in clinical descriptions.

681755.long_answer: Reverse-transcription PCR assays used for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis only need the short segment of viral RNA that lies between the forward and reverse primer binding sites (typically 70–150 nt) to be intact. Global or partial degradation elsewhere in the genome does not interfere with amplification and detection; the reaction will still yield a signal provided the primer/probe sites and the intervening sequence remain undamaged. Therefore the nucleic-acid test is tolerant of RNA degradation so long as the fragment spanning the primer pair is preserved.

698744.long_answer: Published clinical descriptions of Fryns-Aftimos syndrome report characteristic cortical malformations, most notably pachygyria (broad, unusually thick cerebral convolutions). Because this thick-gyral (pachygyric) pattern is a recognized part of the brain phenotype in the syndrome, stating that Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is associated with unusually thick convolutions of the cerebral cortex is accurate. Therefore, it is not incorrect to make that statement.

736626.long_answer:
All three factors listed are recognized causes of microcephaly.

1. MacDermot-Winter syndrome (also termed blepharophimosis-ptosis-microcephaly syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder whose core diagnostic triad includes congenital microcephaly, characteristic eyelid malformations, and developmental delay. Thus, microcephaly is an intrinsic feature of the syndrome.

2. Prenatal alcohol exposure, particularly the spectrum encompassed by fetal alcohol syndrome, disrupts brain growth during gestation. A consistent hallmark of this teratogenic exposure is reduced head circumference at birth and throughout childhood, i.e., microcephaly.

3. Vertically transmitted (congenital) infections—classically grouped as TORCH (toxoplasmosis, “other” such as syphilis and Zika, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) and similar pathogens—can cross the placenta, injure the developing fetal brain, and result in structural abnormalities, including microcephaly. Recent outbreaks of congenital Zika infection dramatically underscored this causal link.

Therefore, MacDermot-Winter syndrome, prenatal alcohol exposure, and vertically transmitted infections are all established etiological factors capable of causing microcephaly.

739348.long_answer: Keloid disorder is characterized by an abnormal fibroproliferative response to virtually any cutaneous injury, including surgical incisions. A heart transplant involves a median sternotomy, chest-tube sites, vascular access lines and repeated endomyocardial biopsy sites—each representing dermal injury. Although transplant recipients receive systemic immunosuppression, these drugs do not eliminate the underlying genetic/biologic propensity for keloid formation. Case reports and small series document keloid development in transplant patients who had a pre-existing tendency. Therefore, individuals with keloid disorder remain at risk—and may in fact have a heightened risk—of developing keloids after a heart transplant. The statement claiming they are “not at risk” is incorrect.

746202.long_answer: Familial intestinal polyatresia syndrome (FIPA) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A gene. TTC7A normally restrains the RhoA/ROCK (Rho-associated co-iled-coil-containing protein kinase) pathway. When TTC7A is defective, RhoA becomes hyper-activated, which in turn increases ROCK kinase activity. Elevated ROCK signaling perturbs the organization of the actin cytoskeleton, leading to failure of apical-basal polarity in intestinal epithelial cells. Restoration of polarity in experimental models can be achieved by pharmacologic inhibition of ROCK, confirming that excessive ROCK activity is the proximal driver of the polarity defect. Therefore, FIPA is indeed associated with increased Rho kinase activity that disrupts epithelial polarity.

759664.long_answer: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation produces DNA damage in keratinocytes, leading to mutations in the TP53 gene. The mutant p53 protein is more stable than the wild-type form, so it accumulates in the cell and is readily detected immunohistochemically. Thus, UV exposure is associated with increased— not reduced— p53 expression in sun-damaged epidermis and in actinic keratosis. The development of actinic keratosis is therefore linked to p53 mutation and overexpression, rather than to a decrease in p53 expression.

762048.long_answer: Cartilage–Hair Hypoplasia (CHH) is a skeletal dysplasia that is frequently accompanied by cellular immunodeficiency. One of its hallmark laboratory abnormalities is chronic lymphopenia, most notably reduced T-cell counts. Reported lymphocyte values in CHH patients often fall below 1.0 × 10⁹/L, sometimes markedly lower. Therefore, an adult who presents with a lymphocyte count of < 0.9 × 10⁹/L could indeed be displaying a hematological sign compatible with CHH, and the disorder should be considered in the differential diagnosis, especially if other clinical features (short stature, fine sparse hair, skeletal anomalies) are present.

779986.long_answer: Mowat-Wilson syndrome is frequently accompanied by epilepsy or other seizure disorders in a large proportion of affected individuals. Because seizures are common, routine electroencephalography (EEG) in these patients often reveals focal or generalized epileptiform discharges or other abnormalities. Therefore, anticipating an abnormal EEG in someone with Mowat-Wilson syndrome is consistent with the clinical experience reported in the literature; expecting such findings is not incorrect.

789625.long_answer: The gene implicated is RAI1 (Retinoic Acid-Induced 1). Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 due to a 17p11.2 deletion causes Smith–Magenis syndrome, whereas a reciprocal 17p11.2 duplication including RAI1 causes Potocki–Lupski syndrome. The RAI1 protein contains a PHD-type zinc-finger domain, a motif that coordinates zinc ions. Consequently, Gene Ontology annotations for RAI1 include the term “metal ion binding.” Therefore, the gene in question is classified as metal ion binding.

799254.long_answer: Pseudo-IUGR (also called constitutional smallness) is reserved for fetuses who are small for gestational age but otherwise healthy, with no underlying pathological process; their small size represents a normal variant. Primordial dwarfism, in contrast, is a genetic growth-failure syndrome that produces marked, proportionate intrauterine growth restriction due to an intrinsic fetal pathology. Because the growth restriction arises from a disease process within the fetus, it is classified as true symmetrical (type I) IUGR, not as pseudo-IUGR. Therefore, a fetus affected by primordial dwarfism is not considered pseudo-IUGR.

808372.long_answer: The classic clinical triad used to recognize primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) includes: (1) primary or secondary amenorrhoea, (2) hyper-gonadotropic hypogonadism, and (3) hypo-oestrogenism. Individuals with 5-α-reductase type 2 deficiency (SRD5A2 gene mutations) are 46,XY and are often raised as females. Because they lack a uterus and ovaries, they invariably present with primary amenorrhoea if they are reared female. Thus the disorder is indeed associated with one component of the POI diagnostic triad—primary amenorrhoea—even though the overall aetiology and pathophysiology differ from true ovarian failure.

814637.long_answer: The GLB1 gene encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-galactosidase. Pathogenic variants in GLB1 cause GM1 gangliosidosis (infantile, juvenile and adult forms) and Morquio-B disease. The other major category, GM2 gangliosidosis (which includes Tay-Sachs disease, Sandhoff disease and GM2 activator deficiency), is produced by defects in different genes—HEXA, HEXB and GM2A, respectively. Thus, GLB1 is responsible for GM1 gangliosidosis only, not for both GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses.

831634.long_answer:
The aortopulmonary space (often referred to as the aortopulmonary window) contains lymph nodes and loose connective tissue situated between the aortic arch and the main pulmonary artery. Any pathological process that produces lymph-node enlargement or soft-tissue masses in the mediastinum can therefore manifest in this space.  
• Infections (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infections, bacterial lymphadenitis) can cause reactive or suppurative enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes, including those in the aortopulmonary window.  
• Autoimmune or granulomatous disorders such as sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or rheumatoid nodules can similarly lead to nodal or soft-tissue involvement in this region.  
• Malignancies—whether primary mediastinal tumors (lymphoma) or metastatic disease (e.g., lung, breast, melanoma)—commonly produce aortopulmonary window lymphadenopathy or mass lesions.  
Therefore, infectious, autoimmune, and neoplastic conditions are all well-recognized causes of abnormal findings in the aortopulmonary space.

836831.long_answer: The inherited disorder that shows a markedly high incidence in the Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean region of Québec is tyrosinemia type I (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency), not tyrosinemia type II. Tyrosinemia type II (caused by tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency) is a rare condition worldwide and has not been reported to occur with increased frequency in this particular population. Therefore, saying that tyrosinemia type II is common in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region is incorrect.

865929.long_answer: Osteopetrosis is characterized by defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, so calcium that would normally be released from bone remains trapped in the skeleton. As a result, patients often develop normal or low (not elevated) serum calcium concentrations and may even experience hypocalcemic tetany, especially in infancy. Persistent serum calcium levels above 10.7 mg/dL (hypercalcemia) are therefore not a recognized consequence of osteopetrosis; the disorder is more commonly associated with low or normal calcium levels.

883181.long_answer: Habermann’s disease (pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, or PLEVA) presents with crops of vesicular, crusted or necrotic papules that closely resemble the lesions of chicken-pox, the highly contagious infection produced by the varicella-zoster virus. Because chicken-pox is far more common and often the first condition physicians think of when they see scattered vesicles and crusts, PLEVA is frequently misidentified as varicella, at least initially, until biopsy or the clinical course clarifies the diagnosis. Thus, in routine clinical practice, Habermann’s disease is indeed often (i.e., commonly) misdiagnosed as chicken-pox, the contagious disease caused by the varicella virus.

894645.long_answer: Myoglobinuria most often results from rhabdomyolysis.  When rhabdomyolysis is caused by traumatic crush injury it can be complicated by acute kidney injury, but contemporary series show overall mortality rates generally ranging from about 10 % to 40 %.  Even in the sickest sub-groups who require dialysis the reported death rate rarely exceeds 50 %.  Therefore, it is not accurate to state that this common cause of myoglobinuria carries a mortality rate greater than 50 % as a matter of established clinical consensus.

904524.long_answer: Abruzzo-Erikson syndrome is an earlier eponym for the condition that is now grouped under CHARGE syndrome (characterised by Coloboma, Heart defects, Choanal atresia, Retarded growth/development, Genital anomalies and Ear anomalies). The great majority of individuals diagnosed with CHARGE/Abruzzo-Erikson syndrome carry heterozygous pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene. Therefore, the syndrome is indeed linked to CHD7 mutation.

910085.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) are strongly recommended in diabetes because they slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy and lower the risk of major cardiovascular events. Low-dose aspirin, on the other hand, is used in diabetes primarily for secondary (and, in selected high-risk patients, primary) prevention of cardiovascular disease; it has no proven benefit in preventing diabetic kidney disease and prolonged use may actually impair renal function. Therefore, while ACEIs help prevent both renal and cardiovascular complications, aspirin is used only for cardiovascular prevention, not for protection against diabetic kidney disease. Consequently, the statement that both ACEIs and aspirin can be used to prevent kidney and cardiovascular diseases caused by diabetes is not correct.

917636.long_answer: There is no information provided in the context about the typical size of nodules in eumycetoma. Because the claim cannot be supported by any data in the supplied context, it cannot be considered factually established.

931338.long_answer: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts primarily on Sertoli cells to promote spermatogenesis, whereas circulating testosterone levels reflect Leydig-cell function driven mainly by luteinizing hormone (LH). Documented cases of FSH-receptor mutations or post-receptor defects show that adult men can have normal LH secretion, normal Leydig-cell responsiveness, and therefore normal to high-normal serum testosterone (e.g., ~630 ng/dL), yet exhibit impaired or absent Sertoli-cell response to FSH. This state—often termed FSH resistance or insensitivity—manifests clinically with normal virilization but defective sperm production. Hence, a normal testosterone concentration does not exclude, and is compatible with, insensitivity to FSH.

933211.long_answer: Pacerone is the brand name for amiodarone, a highly lipophilic class III anti-arrhythmic drug. Because of its strong affinity for lipids, amiodarone and its metabolite desethyl-amiodarone accumulate in alveolar macrophages and type II pneumocytes, producing intracellular phospholipid‐laden ("foamy") macrophages. This drug-induced phospholipidosis manifests pathologically and radiologically as lipoid (lipid) pneumonia, often classified in the literature as an exogenous lipoid pneumonia because the offending lipid-like substance (amiodarone) is introduced from outside the body. Numerous clinical reports and reviews describe “amiodarone-induced lipoid pneumonia” or “amiodarone lung” as a recognized form of pulmonary toxicity. Therefore, it is established that exposure to Pacerone can lead to exogenous lipid (lipoid) pneumonia in susceptible patients.

935298.long_answer: The setting sun sign results from impaired up-gaze caused by pressure on the dorsal midbrain and is classically associated with conditions that raise intracranial pressure—most commonly infantile hydrocephalus or lesions such as tectal tumors. Agenesis of the corpus callosum, by itself, does not produce dorsal midbrain compression or the characteristic oculomotor disturbance needed to create the setting sun phenomenon. Therefore, a patient who has isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum would not be expected to exhibit the setting sun sign unless a separate, pressure-producing pathology (e.g., hydrocephalus) were also present.

936226.long_answer: The physician credited with isolating the hepatitis B surface antigen is Baruch Samuel Blumberg, who identified the so-called “Australia antigen” that proved to be the hepatitis B surface antigen and later shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. Blumberg was married to Jean Hlavacek, not to Veronica Tester. Because the physician who married Veronica Tester was a different individual, the person who isolated the hepatitis B surface antigen and the physician who married Veronica Tester are not the same.

951532.long_answer: Harding’s ataxia (also called autosomal-recessive cerebellar ataxia of late onset, first delineated by Harding in 1981) is distinguished from Friedreich’s ataxia by the absence of systemic metabolic complications such as diabetes mellitus. Patients with Harding’s ataxia generally have normal glucose tolerance, and persistent hyperglycaemia is not part of the recognised clinical picture. Therefore a patient with Harding’s ataxia would not be expected to present with sustained high blood-sugar levels.

954923.long_answer: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is followed, in some survivors, by the sudden appearance of multiple benign melanocytic proliferations such as eruptive lentigines or eruptive melanocytic naevi. These lesions involve pigment-producing skin cells (melanocytes) and are considered a recognised, though uncommon, cutaneous sequela of TEN. Hence a benign eruptive condition of pigment-producing cells can indeed complicate or follow toxic epidermal necrolysis.

955705.long_answer: Infliximab (a chimeric anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody) has regulatory approval for Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis.
