Collagenous colitis – a form of microscopic colitis – is usually managed with antidiarrhoeal agents, budesonide, and occasionally immunomodulators such as azathioprine or methotrexate. Although a few case reports and small series describe off-label use of infliximab in patients with severe, treatment-refractory collagenous colitis, these anecdotal experiences have not led to formal guideline recommendations or regulatory approval. Therefore, infliximab is not an established or officially indicated therapy for collagenous colitis.

961487.long_answer: The World Health Organization (the United Nations health agency) identifies major depressive disorder as the single largest contributor to years lived with disability globally. A substantial body of epidemiological and clinical research shows that habitual or chronic procrastination is positively correlated with higher levels of depressive symptoms and with a greater likelihood of meeting criteria for major depressive disorder. Although procrastination is not itself a clinical diagnosis, it is consistently associated—across cross-sectional studies, longitudinal cohorts, and meta-analyses—with increased depressive mood, anhedonia, and functional impairment characteristic of depression. Therefore, procrastination is indeed associated with the disorder that the WHO lists as the leading cause of disability worldwide.

966492.long_answer: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita involves congenital joint contractures that stem from reduced fetal movement. The diminished movement limits normal muscle and bone growth in the affected extremities. Consequently, the involved limb often has smaller muscle bulk and slower longitudinal growth, leading to observable limb-length discrepancy or a smaller foot on one side. Therefore, it is well-recognized that arthrogryposis can result in one leg or foot being shorter or smaller than the contralateral side.

982027.long_answer: Thalidomide exposure during early pregnancy is indeed a well-established and historically prominent cause of phocomelia. However, management of phocomelia focuses on the malformed or absent limbs (e.g., limb-lengthening procedures, orthopedic surgery, prosthetics, physical and occupational therapy). Surgical intervention on the facial bones is not a recognized or standard treatment for this limb malformation. Therefore, while the causal link to thalidomide is correct, the stated treatment is not; taken together, the overall statement is inaccurate.

998920.long_answer: In syndromes where hypogonadism occurs together with sensorineural hearing loss in females (e.g., Perrault syndrome, Turner syndrome–associated deafness), the hearing deficit results from congenital or progressive inner-ear/cochlear pathology. Because the hair cells and neural elements are damaged or malformed, the deafness does not recover with hormonal correction and is regarded as permanent rather than reversible.

373907.long_answer: Members of the parrot (psittacine) family—roughly 350 extant species of parrots, parakeets, macaws, cockatoos, and related birds—are recognized as common reservoirs of Chlamydia psittaci, the bacterium that causes psittacosis. Thus, the parrot family comprises about 350 species capable of transmitting this zoonotic disease to humans.

264282.long_answer: Behçet’s disease shows a strong genetic association with the HLA-B51 allele. HLA-B51 is a class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) surface molecule encoded at the B locus on chromosome 6, and carriers have a markedly increased risk of developing Behçet’s disease compared with non-carriers.

669273.long_answer: Oculocerebrocutaneous (OCC) syndrome – also called Delleman syndrome – is classically characterized by ocular malformations (e.g., orbital cysts, microphthalmia), cutaneous defects, and a variety of cerebral anomalies. Reported brain findings include agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, porencephalic or arachnoid cysts, cerebral dysplasia, and hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus represents an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the cerebral ventricles, leading to ventricular dilation and potentially increased intracranial pressure. Because hydrocephalus is a documented central-nervous-system manifestation in patients with OCC syndrome, the statement that a buildup of CSF within the brain (which can raise intracranial pressure) is one of the symptoms associated with oculocerebrocutaneous syndrome is consistent with established medical descriptions.

788541.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is marked by a characteristic coarse, thickened facial appearance. The same coarse facial features are a well-recognised hallmark of the Rasopathies—disorders caused by mutations in the Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway such as Costello and cardio-facio-cutaneous syndromes. This shared craniofacial phenotype is the main clinical similarity between Fryns-Aftimos syndrome and conditions stemming from Ras/MAPK signaling defects.

907498.long_answer: Hydroxychloroquine is commonly tried as an early systemic therapy for generalized or recalcitrant granuloma annulare. It is also an established disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for adults with rheumatoid arthritis, prescribed either as monotherapy in mild disease or in combination with methotrexate to enhance therapeutic effect.

339683.long_answer: Sirolimus, an mTOR-inhibiting immunosuppressant originally isolated from the fungus-like actinomycete Streptomyces hygroscopicus, characteristically raises serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Unlike the calcineurin inhibitors cyclosporine and tacrolimus, it does not increase renal vascular resistance, so clinically significant hypertension is uncommon.

809641.long_answer: Infantile malignant (autosomal-recessive) osteopetrosis can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TNFRSF11A gene, which encodes the RANK receptor required for osteoclast differentiation. TNFRSF11A is mapped to the cytogenetic band 18q22.1 on human chromosome 18, matching the chromosomal location specified in the question.

284704.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by mutations in the NBN gene, which resides on human chromosome 8. Chromosome 8 in the current human reference genome spans roughly 145 million nucleotide base pairs, so the chromosome containing the causal gene comprises about 145 Mb of DNA.

794196.long_answer: Post-ictal paresis/paralysis (Todd’s paralysis) follows an epileptic seizure. Benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam and clonazepam are well-established antiepileptic agents; they are first-line drugs for aborting acute seizures and status epilepticus and are also used as adjunctive long-term therapy in some epilepsy syndromes. Because they are routinely employed to control the seizures that give rise to post-ictal paralysis, benzodiazepines are indeed used to manage the underlying disease.

678399.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type 0 results from deficiency of hepatic glycogen synthase (GYS2), an ~80 kDa enzyme that catalyzes transfer of glucose from UDP-glucose to glycogen. Glycogen synthase belongs to the broad glycosyltransferase protein family, enzymes that transfer sugar moieties to acceptor molecules. Thus, the relevant general protein family is the glycosyltransferases.

668585.long_answer: Patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal are routinely given thiamine (vitamin B1) to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamine belongs to the B-complex group of vitamins, all of which are water-soluble. Because thiamine is water-soluble (i.e., readily dissolves in water), the statement that this routinely recommended vitamin is insoluble in water is incorrect.

682791.long_answer: Paul Tessier, a pioneering French cranio-facial surgeon, introduced the first corrective operations for orbital hypertelorism in the 1960s and later devised the widely adopted Tessier craniofacial cleft classification, which includes the spectrum of congenital bifid-nose malformations.

334677.long_answer: Langer–Giedion syndrome (trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II) is produced by a microdeletion on the long arm of chromosome 8, specifically encompassing bands q24.11 through q24.13. Loss of this 8q24.1 segment, which includes the TRPS1 and EXT1 genes, contrasts with Warkany syndrome 2, where an entire extra copy of chromosome 8 is present.

667770.long_answer: Hay-Wells (AEC) syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the TP63 gene. TP63 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q27-q29), so the mutated gene responsible for Hay-Wells syndrome is located on chromosome 3.

139364.long_answer: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) is a rare autosomal-recessive, multisystemic lipid-storage disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in CYP27A1. Accumulation of cholestanol in the central nervous system produces early psychomotor delay and marked slowing of both mental and physical activity, a syndrome that clinically resembles the psychomotor retardation observed in major depressive disorder. Additional systemic features such as juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas and progressive ataxia confirm its multisystemic nature.

527725.long_answer: Cobalamin C (cblC) disease is the prototype inborn error of vitamin B₁₂ processing in which conversion of cobalamin to its active co-factor methylcobalamin is blocked. Loss of methylcobalamin cripples methionine synthase, leading to homocystinuria, megaloblastic anemia, and combined neurologic-developmental abnormalities such as intellectual disability, seizures, hypotonia, and growth delay. The syndrome therefore presents with mental retardation, anemia, and other neurological and developmental problems characteristic of impaired methylcobalamin metabolism.

118785.long_answer: The term “Fetal Alcohol Effect” (FAE) was once applied to children whose brains were damaged by prenatal alcohol exposure, but who lacked the full facial or growth features of fetal alcohol syndrome. Because it was imprecise and overlapped with other diagnoses, the term has largely been abandoned in favor of the broader, better-defined category Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), which includes alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND) and other subtypes.

439326.long_answer: Papillorenal (renal-coloboma) syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in the PAX2 gene. PAX2 is one of the nine human genes that share the conserved paired-box DNA-binding domain, placing it within the Paired box (PAX) transcription factor gene family.

165936.long_answer: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular allergic disorder that shares the immunopathology of other type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions. In this mechanism, IgE antibodies bind to mast cells; upon exposure to relevant allergens, cross-linking of the surface-bound IgE triggers mediator release and produces the characteristic signs and symptoms. Among the five major immunoglobulin isotypes found in human serum (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE), IgE is present at the lowest concentration, making it the least abundant isotype. Because vernal keratoconjunctivitis is mediated predominantly by IgE, it indeed involves the least abundant antibody isotype.

406747.long_answer: Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis often arises in chronic infections such as osteomyelitis. Diabetic patients, particularly those with diabetic foot ulcers, have a high incidence of osteomyelitis. The chronic inflammatory stimulus of osteomyelitis elevates interleukin-6, boosts thrombopoietin production, and drives a reactive elevation of platelet count, linking this condition both to reactive thrombocythemia and to diabetes.

998849.long_answer: Multinucleated, striated skeletal muscle fibres rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis. Their predominant lactate dehydrogenase isoenzyme is composed of four ‘M’ (muscle) subunits, designated LDH-5 (M4). This form efficiently converts pyruvate to lactate under low-oxygen conditions, matching the metabolic demands of skeletal muscle tissue that contains repeating sarcomeres.

925519.long_answer: The congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD) deficiency blocks conversion of 17α-hydroxypregnenolone to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, leading to markedly elevated 17α-hydroxypregnenolone levels. Because both androgen and glucocorticoid synthesis are impaired, XY fetuses are undervirilized and XX fetuses may be virilized by accumulated Δ5 steroids, producing ambiguous genitalia in both genetic sexes.

0.long_answer: Albers-Schönberg disease is the benign, autosomal-dominant form of osteopetrosis (marble-bone disease). It results from defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, so bone is laid down but not properly remodelled. Radiographically the skeleton shows uniformly dense, ‘bone-within-bone’ or ‘sandwich vertebra’ appearances. Clinically, bones are abnormally hard yet brittle, predisposing to pathological fractures; some patients develop cranial-nerve compression, mild anaemia, or osteomyelitis of the mandible, but overall the course is relatively mild compared with the malignant infantile form.

353225.long_answer: Macrosomia (excessive prenatal or postnatal over-growth) is a hallmark feature of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, a congenital overgrowth disorder. Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome have a well-established, markedly increased risk of embryonal tumors, most notably Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Therefore, individuals who exhibit macrosomia in the context of this syndrome are recognized as being predisposed to, and may indeed present with, Wilms tumor.

1.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome, formally called acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II, is a rare autosomal-recessive craniosynostosis disorder most often caused by pathogenic variants in RAB23 or MEGF8. Premature fusion of multiple skull sutures produces an acrocephalic (tower-shaped) head, and patients typically show polysyndactyly (extra, fused digits) together with brachydactyly (short fingers and toes). Other frequent manifestations include facial anomalies (flat nasal bridge, low-set or malformed ears), obesity or short stature, congenital heart defects, genital or anal malformations, and varying degrees of developmental delay or intellectual disability.

592016.long_answer: The clinical manifestations seen in mucolipidosis I (ML I)—for example coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, skeletal dysostosis, cherry-red macular spot, and myoclonic seizures—are not unique to this disorder. Similar constellations of signs are encountered in several other inborn errors of metabolism, including the mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler and Hunter syndromes), GM2 gangliosidoses (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff), sialidoses, and other lysosomal storage diseases. Consequently, the symptoms of ML I do indeed occur in other metabolic disorders, and a definitive diagnosis relies on specific biochemical or molecular testing rather than clinical features alone.

2.long_answer: The question refers to 'that gene,' but no specific gene has been identified in the provided information. Without knowing which gene is being discussed, its normal physiological function cannot be accurately described.

1.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive disorder is called DOOR syndrome, an acronym for its hallmark findings: congenital sensorineural Deafness, nail abnormalities (Onychodystrophy), bony malformations of the hands and feet (Osteodystrophy), and intellectual disability (formerly termed mental Retardation). Many affected individuals also develop seizures, further defining the clinical picture.

357263.long_answer: Strumpell-Lorrain disease is the classic name for hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), a group of genetically determined neurodegenerative disorders in which length-dependent degeneration of the corticospinal tracts (and often dorsal columns) produces a slowly progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs. It usually presents in childhood or early adulthood, most often with an autosomal-dominant inheritance (e.g., SPAST/SPG4 mutations), and is characterized clinically by bilateral leg stiffness, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, and a spastic, scissoring gait; bowel–bladder urgency and mild sensory loss may occur. “Pure” HSP involves chiefly these pyramidal signs, while “complicated” forms may include ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, cognitive impairment, or other neurologic features.

360820.long_answer: DC-SIGN (Dendritic Cell-Specific ICAM-3-Grabbing Non-integrin) is a C-type lectin receptor on dendritic cells and certain macrophages. It recognizes high-mannose glycans on viral envelope proteins; West Nile virus exploits this by binding its envelope glycoprotein to DC-SIGN, which functions as an attachment/entry factor that concentrates the virus on the cell surface and facilitates its internalization into host cells.

1.long_answer: The gene LGALS3BP was originally identified as the gene whose product was termed 90K/Thespin. Molecular characterization showed that this gene encodes a secreted glycoprotein that specifically associates with the lectin galectin-3; the accepted name for this protein is Galectin-3-binding protein (also known as Mac-2-binding protein or 90K).

413785.long_answer: The TUBB gene encodes β-tubulin, one of the two obligatory subunits of microtubules. Microtubules polymerise to build the mitotic spindle—the cytoskeletal apparatus that attaches to kinetochores and pulls sister chromatids to opposite poles during anaphase. Loss or disruption of TUBB prevents microtubule formation, abolishing spindle assembly and thereby blocking chromatid separation in cell division.

627537.long_answer: Approximately one-third of people with Klippel–Feil syndrome exhibit Sprengel deformity—a congenital elevation and malrotation of the scapula caused by incomplete caudal migration of the scapular anlage during embryogenesis. Clinical studies consistently report this scapular anomaly in about 25–40 % (commonly cited as ~30 %) of Klippel–Feil cases, making it one of the most frequent associated conditions.

2.long_answer: ICF syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in ZBTB24, a gene that encodes a transcriptional repressor with a POZ (BTB) domain followed by multiple C2H2 zinc-finger motifs. This POZ/zinc-finger protein normally participates in chromatin repression; its loss disturbs DNA methylation at pericentromeric repeats, producing the characteristic immunodeficiency, centromeric instability and congenital facial anomalies of the disorder.

655628.long_answer: Members of the type II cytokine receptor family (e.g., interferon-α/β, interferon-γ, and IL-10 family receptors) lack intrinsic catalytic domains and therefore rely on associated Janus kinases. Upon ligand binding, receptor subunits heterodimerize, bringing together JAK1, JAK2, and/or TYK2 that are constitutively bound to their cytoplasmic tails; these kinases trans-phosphorylate each other and the receptor, initiating downstream STAT signaling. Thus, the Janus kinases JAK1, JAK2, and TYK2 are the principal kinases that mediate signaling for type II cytokine receptors.

523257.long_answer: The question does not specify which hormone is being referred to, and no contextual details are provided from which to infer it. Therefore, the year of first isolation cannot be determined from the given information.

3.long_answer: Nebulin runs alongside the actin (thin) filament from the Z-disk toward the pointed end and acts as a molecular ruler, so its own length is essentially identical to—and thereby determines—the length of the thin filament.

426619.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I (also known as sialidosis) results from deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase (sialidase). The enzyme defect leads to intralysosomal accumulation of sialyl-oligosaccharides and related substrates, a hallmark feature of the broader group of lysosomal storage disorders. Consequently, in medical classification systems and in the scientific literature, Mucolipidosis type I is explicitly categorized as a lysosomal storage disease.

120745.long_answer: The most prevalent autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia is SPG4, caused by pathogenic variants in the SPAST (spastin) gene. SPG4 accounts for roughly 40–50% of dominant HSP cases worldwide, making it the commonest form of AD spastic paraplegia.

654787.long_answer: Keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome is a rare, inherited ectodermal dysplasia characterized by the triad of progressive vascularizing keratitis of the cornea, ichthyosiform or hyperkeratotic skin lesions, and congenital sensorineural deafness. 732795.long_answer: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), located in the anterior hypothalamus, serves as the brain’s master circadian pacemaker. 215035.long_answer: In the classic amnestic (or amnesic) syndrome—produced by bilateral damage to the medial temporal lobe or diencephalic memory circuits—patients show profound anterograde amnesia and a retrograde amnesia that is temporally graded: recent autobiographical memories are lost while more remote memories are relatively spared. 487758.long_answer: The LIS1 gene, officially named PAFAH1B1, encodes the microtubule- and dynein-binding protein LIS1 that regulates cytoplasmic dynein–driven transport during neuronal migration. 205706.long_answer: Low circulating levels of the anticoagulant Protein C are repeatedly found in patients who go on to develop acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), especially in the context of sepsis or major trauma. 326041.long_answer: Grebe-type chondrodysplasia (acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type) is a skeletal dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 gene. 3.long_answer: Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive congenital myopathy marked by congenital facial paralysis, Pierre Robin sequence, generalized muscle hypotonia and weakness. 685009.long_answer: Lipoid proteinosis, also known as Urbach–Wiethe disease, is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ECM1 gene. 1.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is an autosomal-dominant disorder of skeletal-muscle excitability produced by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A gene that encodes the Nav1.4 voltage-gated sodium channel. Its hallmark is myotonia (delayed relaxation) that is triggered and WORSENS with repeated muscle contractions or exposure to cold—termed paradoxical myotonia, because, unlike classic myotonia, it does not warm-up but instead intensifies. After prolonged activity, patients can develop transient flaccid weakness. 819839.long_answer: Cor triatriatum dexter is a rare congenital defect produced when the right venous (sinus) valve fails to regress completely. The persistent valve forms a membrane that partitions the right atrium—where the coronary sinus (and its Thebesian valve) is also located—into two chambers, giving the heart three atrial cavities.

803647.long_answer: Alzheimer’s disease accounts for roughly 60–70 % of dementia cases worldwide. Recent research has detected the oral pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis—bacteria commonly implicated in gingivitis and periodontitis—and its neurotoxic gingipain enzymes in the brains and cerebrospinal fluid of Alzheimer’s patients, linking this bacterium to the neurodegenerative process characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease.

227907.long_answer: When ocular inflammation is suspected to be a masquerade syndrome and infectious or autoimmune uveitis has been excluded, molecular analysis of the vitreous humor is performed. 669126.long_answer: Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) is characterized by progressive deposition of glycosaminoglycans in multiple tissues, including the meninges and arachnoid villi. This can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and lead to communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus in affected children. When clinically significant hydrocephalus develops, the standard management is neurosurgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid—most commonly placement of a ventriculoperitoneal or ventriculoatrial shunt. Therefore, it is accurate to state that children with Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome may develop hydrocephalus and that the condition is typically treated with surgery.

646794.long_answer: Microsporidia are obligate intracellular pathogens that are normally controlled by CD4⁺ T-cell–mediated immunity. 415751.long_answer: In Chédiak-Higashi syndrome the defective neutrophil function leads to recurrent pyogenic infections characterized by a purulent (suppurative) exudate—commonly referred to as pus—composed mainly of neutrophils, necrotic cells and edema fluid.

532019.long_answer: Hers disease, formally designated glycogen storage disease type VI, was first characterized by Henri-Géry Hers in 1959. Owing to its hepatic glycogen-phosphorylase deficiency, it causes hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia and elevated transaminases—clinical findings that closely mimic those of glycogen storage disease type III. Consequently, GSD VI is a standard consideration in the differential diagnosis of suspected GSD III cases.

224062.long_answer: The SPAST gene, encoding the microtubule-severing AAA ATPase spastin, is the major cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia. Pathogenic variants in SPAST (also called SPG4) explain roughly 40–50 % of all genetically resolved HSP cases, reflecting its central role among AAA protein family members in axonal maintenance.

742501.long_answer: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), is a rare and highly aggressive mature T-cell malignancy. Patients typically present with generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly due to widespread nodal and extranodal infiltration. Unlike adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, PTCL-NOS is characteristically negative for human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), helping distinguish it from HTLV-1–associated T-cell neoplasms.

969034.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the coding region of the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene are an established cause of holoprosencephaly (HPE). Limb malformations such as polydactyly or polysyndactyly, however, are typically produced by gain-of-function alterations confined to a distant limb-specific enhancer of SHH (the ZRS) or by mutations in downstream pathway genes such as GLI3 or GLI2. 853329.long_answer: Barth syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TAZ gene, which encodes the mitochondrial phospholipid-remodeling enzyme tafazzin. 281839.long_answer: The only Foix-Chavany-Marie (opercular) syndrome whose deficits are completely reversible is the post-ictal/epileptic variant. 351187.long_answer: Atoh1, also known as Math1, is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that has been proposed to act as a tumor suppressor in several cancers. Adenoviral delivery of Atoh1 into the developing cochlea of embryonic mice drives supporting cells to trans-differentiate into mechanosensory hair cells, leading to robust hair-cell growth. 703052.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome has been documented in Papua New Guinea. 747234.long_answer: Liver transplantation (orthotopic liver transplant) replaces the cirrhotic liver with a healthy donor organ, abolishing portal hypertension and thereby treating esophageal varices. 142759.long_answer: Bevacizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). It received U.S. FDA approval in 2004 for use with 5-fluorouracil–based chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer. 378607.long_answer: Polysaccharides of the glycosaminoglycan family are grouped into four major classes—hyaluronan, chondroitin/dermatan sulfates, heparin/heparan sulfate, and keratan sulfate—according to the composition and linkage pattern of their repeating core disaccharide units. 485815.long_answer: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is routinely given to patients withdrawing from alcohol because chronic alcohol use impairs thiamine absorption and storage, placing them at high risk for thiamine deficiency. Adequate thiamine levels are essential for cerebral glucose metabolism; deficiency leads to the classic neurologic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion). 114428.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene. Cytogenetic mapping shows BCOR resides on the short arm of the X-chromosome at band p11.4, making Xp11.4 the chromosomal location of the gene mutated in OFCD syndrome.

991013.long_answer: Patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma frequently report so-called B symptoms, one of which is severe, profuse nocturnal sweating. Clinically, these episodes are termed “drenching night sweats,” indicating perspiration intense enough to soak sleepwear or bed linens.

421078.long_answer: L-carnitine is routinely supplemented in propionic acidemia because it shuttles long-chain fatty acyl groups across the mitochondrial inner membrane via the carnitine shuttle, allowing β-oxidation and ATP generation while also forming propionyl-carnitine that can be excreted, thereby lowering toxic propionyl-CoA levels.

571485.long_answer: The panniculus adiposus is the dense layer of subcutaneous fatty tissue in the lower abdomen. After rapid weight loss it can overhang as a panniculus, and in diseases such as deep morphea (morphea profunda) this fat layer may become inflamed (panniculitis) or undergo sclerosis.

821517.long_answer: Hereditary retinoschisis, most often the X-linked juvenile form, is produced by pathogenic mutations in the RS1 gene on Xp22.2. RS1 encodes retinoschisin, a secreted cell-adhesion protein that stabilizes the interaction between photoreceptors and bipolar cells. 144821.long_answer: Eosinophilic folliculitis is strongly associated with HIV infection and is most often seen in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), a condition marked by progressive loss of CD4⁺ T-cells and consequent immune system failure.

583155.long_answer: In type I (distal) renal tubular acidosis, the α-intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct fail to secrete hydrogen ions via their H⁺-ATPase/H⁺-K⁺-ATPase pumps. • DPP-4 inhibitors (e.g., sitagliptin) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) – enhance incretin activity, lower glucose and can improve fatigue/polydipsia related to hyperglycaemia.
• SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin) – promote renal glucose excretion, decrease blood glucose and improve symptomatic polyuria/polydipsia over time.
• Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone) – improve insulin sensitivity and thereby alleviate hyperglycaemia-related symptoms.
The collective evidence and clinical guidelines confirm that these medications are effective in controlling blood glucose levels and, by extension, alleviating the symptoms attributable to uncontrolled diabetes. Hence, the statement that diabetes medications are known to alleviate symptoms of the condition is supported by broad biomedical consensus.
